The Middle Ages are generally defined in relation 
to the place they occupy between the classical   civilizations of Greece and Rome, and the modern 
era beginning with the Renaissance, so let’s start   with the end of the ancient Mediterranean world. 
This was centered around the two halves of a Roman   empire that stretched from Spain in the west to 
Mesopotamia in the east, and from central Europe   in the north to north Africa in the south. By the 
6th century CE, the eastern empire had developed   into an independent state now called “Byzantine” 
after its capital Constantinople, which had once   been known as Byzantium. Meanwhile the western 
empire had splintered into separate kingdoms   ruled by the various Germanic tribes: eastern and 
western Goths, Vandals, Franks, and Huns, which by   the 5th and 6th centuries had pushed into Italy, 
France, Spain, and north Africa. These tribes   became part of the Roman-Celtic world, helping 
to create a new fusion of languages and cultures.  Italy, which had been the heartland of the western 
Empire, was conquered in the late 5th century by   the eastern Goth Theodoric the Great, who also 
took Spain and southern France from other Germanic   tribes. But rather than declaring his kingdom an 
independent state, he recognized the superiority   of the Byzantine emperor, who still claimed to 
be the emperor of Rome. He respected the laws   issued by the imperial court, and the traditional 
Roman aristocracy embodied in the Senate continued   to play a role in the kingdom’s administration. 
Roman law was also maintained, though it applied   only to Roman citizens, while the Goths were 
governed by their own set of rules. Traditional   Roman culture was also respected to some degree, 
and in addition to classical Latin literature,   which continued to be read, there was some new 
work produced by men like the scholar Cassiodorus,   who created an educational program which 
combined Christian and classical philosophy;   and the Stoic philosopher Boethius, who wrote the 
Consolation of Philosophy, which became one of   the most popular books of the Middle Ages.
After Theodoric’s death, there was a war   between his successors and the Byzantine Empire 
which ended in 554, when the emperor Justinian   incorporated Italy into his domains. But after he 
died in 565, Italy came under the rule of another   Germanic tribe, the Lombards. The Lombard king 
was not hereditary but was chosen by his dukes,   who were fairly independent of the royal court. 
Over the next few centuries, the Lombards   came to speak Latin and adopted Roman cultural 
practices. They converted from the Arian church,   a type of Christianity which the German tribes 
had embraced, to the Catholicism of Rome. Then in   the late 8th century, the Lombards lost control 
of Italy to the Frankish king Charlemagne, or   Charles the Great. The Franks had dominated Gaul 
since their king Clovis took it from the Romans in   the late 5th century. But Charlemagne, who founded 
the dynasty now called “Carolingian” in his honor,   conquered southern France and most of Germany. He 
also launched attacks into Spain, which had been   a Visigothic kingdom but was conquered by Muslim 
forces in the early 8th century. The defeat his   armies suffered there was the basis for one 
of the most popular pieces of literature of   the later Middle Ages, the Song of Roland.
Charlemagne’s kingdom became the Holy Roman   Empire in the year 800, and he was crowned as 
its emperor by Pope Leo III. This amounted to an   acknowledgment of the Catholic Church’s authority 
to appoint secular kings, and a challenge to the   authority of the Byzantine emperor, who for 300 
years had been the only official ruler of Rome.   The idea that the Church could wield political 
power theoretically contradicted the doctrine that   the Pope and the emperor had their own spheres 
of authority. But in practice the Church was a   wealthy land-owning institution that intervened 
in politics, and expected the obedience of the   bishops and priests who served in the various 
kingdoms of Europe. In fact, a document called   the “Donation of Constantine”, which was proven 
during the Renaissance to have been a forgery,   was claimed during the Middle Ages to be a formal 
acknowledgment that this fourth-century emperor,   and his successors after him, recognized the 
superior authority of the Church. At the same   time, kings often tried to exert control 
over the churches in their territories, and   these conflicts between Popes and kings continued 
until the establishment of secular nation-states   early in the modern period. The laws of the 
Franks, including the dynasty of Charlemagne,   divided a father’s property among his sons rather 
than giving all of it to the eldest. And although   Charlemagne had only one son, Louis, he had three 
sons who divided the family’s territories between   them in the Treaty of Verdun in 841. This created 
separate kingdoms out of the regions which would   later become France, Germany, northern Italy, 
and the Netherlands. It was also common among   the Franks to divide political power among 
several kings of equal status, while the title   of emperor continued to be held by a single man.
The court of Charlemagne and his successors,   which was based at the German city of Aachen, 
initiated a series of innovations in education   and artistic production which are now known as the 
“Carolingian Renaissance”. The educational reforms   were a response to the fact that many members of 
the clergy were unable to read, or more precisely   to read Latin. This meant that they could not read 
the Bible for themselves or teach it to others.   There was also a lack of scribes who could copy 
the Christian and classical texts written in that   language. Schools were therefore founded 
to instruct priests, and boys who might   become priests, in classical Latin language and 
literature. This initiative was aided by the fact   that, beginning in the 7th century, schools were 
being established in western Europe by monks from   Ireland, whose practice of Christianity centered 
around the reading, copying, and teaching of both   Christian and classical literature. Both the Irish 
monks and the Carolingian court also engaged in   the creation of colorful illustrated manuscripts, 
such as the 9th-century Book of Kells.  The Carolingian educational reform was aided 
by the development of a clear, efficient,   and standardized style of handwriting 
which came to be known as minuscule,   because it used lower-case letters, unlike the 
capital letters which had originally been used   for carving inscriptions in stone. Minuscule and 
later “bookhands” were designed for the copyists   who worked in the scriptoria or writing-rooms 
of monasteries. While their ancient predecessors   wrote on papyrus scrolls, the Christian scribes 
of the Middle Ages used the codex, a set of   parchment pages bound into a book which had first 
become popularized as the form in which copies of   the New Testament were written. The Carolingians 
also invited to Aachen a number of the important   writers, poets, and philosophers of the time, 
most notably the English monk Alcuin of York   and the Irish theologian John Scotus Eriugena.
The collapse of the Roman Empire’s western half,   and the dangers posed by invasions from 
the north, brought an end to the economic   sophistication of previous centuries, which 
had been based upon the Mediterranean sea   trade and the land routes that connected the 
Empire’s eastern edge with Persia, India,   and China. It also depended on the fact that it 
was generally safe for merchants to travel beyond   their own cities in order to buy or sell goods.
The wide variety of commodities that had been   traded across the Empire, from Britain to 
Mesopotamia, disappeared after the 5th century,   and the number of shipwrecks found from the early 
Middle Ages, which has been used as an indicator   of the amount of shipping that was taking 
place, is much smaller than the finds of earlier   centuries. This suggests that the people who 
had been making goods for export, like textiles,   spices, glassware, metalwork, and fine crafts, no 
longer had a financial incentive to produce them,   and agricultural production, which had always 
been the occupation of most people, became even   more important. While in the past, huge amounts 
of grain and other foodstuffs had been grown   in places like Egypt and Sicily to supply the 
inhabitants of enormous cities like Rome, food was   now being grown for local consumption, or bartered 
for other local products rather than being sold   for money. This led to the growth of agricultural 
estates which were mostly self-sufficient,   as large cities began to disappear or become 
much smaller. Rome itself became a town of 20,000   people, and in some places, the entire population 
moved into what had been the amphitheater where   their ancestors held public games, because its 
walls provided them with protection. Some of these   changes may have had to do with an outbreak in the 
6th century, of the same bubonic plague that would   attack Europe in the 14th century. This outbreak, 
the so-called “Plague of Justinian”, killed up to   a quarter of the population of the Mediterranean, 
Europe, and the Middle East. The shrinking of the   European economy was somewhat reversed under the 
Carolingian empire, which united a large area   of western Europe where the roads were safe for 
merchants, and new centers of business began to   appear there. At the same time, the invasions of 
the past 300 years were finally coming to an end,   as nomadic tribes settled into permanent homes 
in places like France, Britain, and Hungary.  The imperial court of Charlemagne and his 
successors was more centralized, and had a   more developed administration, than the Frankish 
courts that preceded it. His empire was divided   into counties, each one governed by a count. But 
these counts were not generally appointed directly   by the emperor, and were not under his immediate 
control, while the Frankish tradition of holding   assemblies of nobles to make important decisions 
limited the emperor’s personal authority. Though   Charlemagne’s main court was at Aachen, he and 
his successors moved among a series of palaces   he had built in different cities so that he could 
maintain contact with the local nobility. There   was also a general meeting once a year which was 
attended by nobles from throughout the empire.   The decisions the emperor reached together with 
his assemblies were recorded in documents called   capitularies, which were not laws but directives 
that the court wanted to be carried out,   though it had no way of enforcing its policies 
other than the oaths of loyalty that the emperor’s   subjects swore to him. The Carolingian empire 
continued to thrive until the late 9th century,   when it was undermined by the attacks of Vikings 
from the north, Hungarians from the east,   and Muslims from Spain who attacked its 
holdings in southern France; and its economic   and military achievements declined along with it.
The Franks already had a written legal code called   the Salic law, which was first commissioned by 
Clovis, and this code became one of the sources   of later European law. But unlike that law, the 
Frankish system of justice relied upon fines for   both civil and criminal offenses, and in cases of 
murder or injury, the family of the perpetrator   paid the family of the victim a weregeld, an 
amount of money determined by the victim’s social   rank. There was no central police power or system 
of courts, and feuds were common as families took   matters into their own hands. In practice, the 
administration of justice, and political authority   in general, was left to the owners of the estates 
or manors that arose in this period. These men,   the lords, were served by vassals who pledged 
their personal loyalty to them and served   them as soldiers in wartime. In return for their 
loyalty, soldiers were rewarded not with a salary,   as had been the case under the later Empire, but 
with a fief or parcel of land which was worked by   serfs. These were farmers who, though they were 
not slaves, were bound by law to remain on the   manor where they were entitled to the protection 
of the lord, and were allowed to keep a portion   of the produce they grew. This system of personal 
loyalty, which was cemented by the formal oaths   that were sworn by the vassals and serfs, has 
been named “feudalism” by modern historians   after feudum, the Latin word for a fiefdom.
Along with the manors, communities grew up in   the early Middle Ages around the monasteries which 
were being founded as centers of scholarship and   religious devotion, and were attracting people who 
disliked the politics and corruption associated   with the higher levels of the Church’s hierarchy. 
The first monastic community was founded in the   6th century by the Roman scholar Cassiodorus, and 
a group of monasteries was established around the   same time by the Italian monk Benedict, who 
wrote a set of rules for the men living in   his communities and others like them, which 
would come to serve as a model for medieval   monastic life. One of the most important scholars 
of the early Middle Ages was an English monk, the   8th-century historian and theologian named Bede.
The early medieval period is generally defined   as ending around the year 1000. This demarcation 
reflects a number of changes. The shifting borders   of the Carolingian era gave way to the larger 
and more lasting kingdoms of France, Germany,   and England. Population size, land use, and 
trade began to steadily increase. The conflicts   between the Christian and Muslim worlds, and 
between the Catholic and Orthodox churches,   reached a head with the outbreak of the Crusades. 
So let’s move forward to the High Middle Ages.

## 3. Latin Vocabulary: Roman Dwellings
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 4K | **Date:** 4 days ago | **Duration:** 5:37 | **ID:** zX3wjxhsz0M
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=zX3wjxhsz0M

### Transcript:
We’ve learned about how the Romans ate and 
dressed, but how did the Romans live? What   were their homes like? If you were a farmer 
in ancient Rome, you would live in a villa.   Unlike what your intuition might tell you, 
a villa-ae was not a wealthy dwelling, but   rather just a farmhouse. A large family house for 
the master and his family, called villa dominica,   was normally sided by pars rustica or farm 
buildings for the animals and the people   taking care of the animals. Sometimes even a 
pars fructuāria would be present. That would   be an orchard of fruit trees and buildings 
for making wine and olive oil. All in all,   it appeared like something very similar to 
what is called a hacienda in Latin America.  Even in the city, common people didn’t have a 
glamorous life. They would all live packed in   apartment buildings called insulae-ārum. This is 
the same word that in Latin normally means island.   These buildings were small, cold, and damp in the 
winter, and steamy hot in the summer. Sometimes   they were large enough to house an entire city 
block, but that didn’t mean more comfortable   living. It just meant a greater concentration of 
people, sometimes with an entire family in one   room. The insulae were poorly built and because 
of that they often collapsed. Other times they   simply burned down or were flooded by the River 
Tiber. The ground floor was often dedicated to   shops called tabernae-ārum, while the apartments 
would be found on the upper floors, up to six or   seven stories. Counterintuitively, the uppermost 
floors were the less desirable ones because of   safety issues. They were usually the cheapest. 
Often they didn’t even have running water,   and that meant no bathrooms were present either. 
So Romans had to leave their apartments in order   to use lātrīnae-ārum, which were public bathrooms 
in the street, and it wasn’t unusual for them   to throw refuse out of their windows, with all 
the associated sanitary issues you can imagine.  Not far from these buildings were the homes of the 
very wealthy. They were called domus-ūs, a single   family dwelling. These houses might include a 
taberna facing the street in order to conduct   business, or to store items not suitable for the 
house. The door or entrance - ōstium was always   from the street. Inside the house you would first 
see a foyer or vestibule, vestibulum-ī, where the   owner would greet visitors. This would lead to 
the internal part of the house - ātrium-iī through   a small hallway - faucēs-ium. The ātrium had 
enclosed rooms on all sides and a compluvium-iī,   an inward-sloping open roof to provide both light 
and shade. This open roof also had the purpose of   collecting precious rain water into a little pool 
- impluvium-iī. Sometimes a small altar called   larārium-iī was present, with the house protector 
gods, Lāres. A tablīnum-ī would serve both as the   study room for the pater familias, the head of 
the house, or as a reception room. The house would   have a lovely internal garden - peristȳlium-iī 
often decorated with a colonnade - porticus-ūs   to help air circulation on those hot summer days. 
Here is where the owner would grow flowers such as   roses - rosa-ae and white lilies - līlium-iī.
A large room was dedicated to dining and   entertaining - trīclīnium-iī. A kitchen - 
culīna-ae would be present for cooking, and   several bedrooms - cubiculum-ī would accommodate 
family and guests. These were usually small,   just the necessary space to accommodate a bed. A 
larger house would also have room for a vegetable   garden - hortus-ī to grow items essential for 
cooking. The interior walls were plastered and   decorated with beautiful paintings of mythology or 
countryside, while floors were often covered with   mosaics - opus vermīculātum made with small tiles 
- tessera-ae. Surprisingly there was not much   furniture, with this being limited to couches, to 
relax or have dinner, as well as tables and chests   to store things. When the weather was particularly 
cold or damp, these homes were made comfortable   by the use of braziers -foculus-ī designed to 
hold hot coals which could be moved conveniently   from room to room if necessary. In order to light 
the house candles, lamps, and torches were used.  The most beautiful examples of domus, extremely 
well preserved, can be admired today in the town   of Pompeii. Villa of the Mysteries, the House 
of Menander, and the House of the Faun are great   examples. And with that, we have a better sense 
of how the Ancient Romans lived in their homes.

**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 4K | **Date:** 11 days ago | **Duration:** 9:06 | **ID:** c_kVr-fhBns

With some general information regarding 
amphibians covered, it’s now time to   explore the diversity of this clade. Let’s 
begin by covering the orders Gymnophiona,   or Apoda, followed by Caudata, or Urodela.
Members of order Gymnophiona are commonly   referred to as caecilians. They are limbless, 
serpent-like amphibians highly adapted to   burrowing, that at first glance resemble giant 
earthworms, though they are not closely related   to earthworms or snakes. All known species have 
small or nonexistent eyes and live mainly hidden   in soil or streambeds, though some, like the two 
members of genus Typhlonectes, are likely fully   aquatic. Regardless, all members of this order are 
noted for their cryptic lifestyle that makes them   difficult to study and understand. They are often 
regarded as the least familiar of all amphibians,   though they range widely in the tropics of 
Central and South America, Southern Asia,   and parts of Africa. In total, there are only 
around 220 confirmed extant species separated   into 10 families, though some of these species 
are known from only a few individuals and their   population sizes are often poorly understood, as 
is their evolution, since their fossil record is   very sparse. All known species are carnivorous 
and diet varies by class, but often includes   earthworms, termites, larval insects, and eggs.
In terms of morphology, the caecilians are noted   not only for their limbless and elongated bodies 
but also for their small mouths and specialized   skulls which are greatly simplified and compact 
compared to other amphibians, and includes a   specialization of the lower jaw as well as an 
inset row of secondary teeth that runs parallel   to the primary teeth. They also possess a unique 
pair of sensory structures known as tentacles,   which are located on either side of the head 
between the eyes and nostrils, likely used for   olfaction. In addition to their skulls and bodies, 
their skin is also unique among amphibians because   of the presence of calcite scales which 
are absent in some families. Regardless,   in most species the skin is smooth, dark, moist, 
and often contains numerous ring-shaped folds,   or annuli, that give them a somewhat 
segmented appearance. Like other amphibians,   their skin also contains a toxin that helps to 
deter predators, but unlike all other amphibians,   some mothers of caecilians allow their young to 
feed on that skin to aid in their development.  In terms of reproduction, caecilians are the 
only order of amphibians to exclusively rely   on internal fertilization. Male caecilians 
have a long tube-like intromittent organ,   the phallodeum, which is inserted into 
the cloaca of the female for two to three   hours. Once fertilized, some species 
lay eggs and subsequently guard them,   though most species are viviparous, meaning 
they give birth to already-developed offspring.   To help these young develop they are fed with 
cells lining the oviduct, which the young eat   with their scraping teeth during development. 
Parental care is common in the caecilians,   and some like the Taita Mountains caecilian feed 
their young by developing an outer layer of skin,   high in fat and other nutrients, which 
the young peel off with modified teeth.  There is some disagreement between the use of 
Caudata or Urodela to describe the extant tailed   amphibians commonly referred to as salamanders. 
Sometimes the terms are used interchangeably,   but sometimes Caudata is treated as the 
crown group and Urodela as the order of   extant species only. As of 2024, the majority 
of textbooks still use Caudata to refer to   extant species so that’s what we will do 
here, but this may change in the future.  This order is often characterized by their 
lizard-like appearance, though they are not   closely related to lizards, with slender bodies, 
blunt snouts, and short limbs that protrude at   right angles from the body. Their skin lacks 
scales, and is moist except in the newts of   Salamandridae, which may have velvety or warty 
skin. Depending on the species, the skin may be   drab or brightly colored, and some have intricate 
patterns of spots, stripes, bars, or blotches.   Most species have four toes on their front limbs 
and five toes on their hind limbs. Some species   are fully aquatic throughout their lives, like 
the axolotls and mudpuppies, while others take   to water intermittently, and others are entirely 
terrestrial as adults. As a group they are noted   for their ability to regenerate lost limbs and 
other parts of their bodies such as their tails,   and many species can drop their tails as a 
defense mechanism known as autotomy. However,   this isn’t their only defense mechanism. Though 
most salamanders are quite small and slow-moving,   many do secrete a mucus that makes them slimy 
and difficult to catch, along with toxins that   vary in toxicity from essentially harmless to 
perhaps the most toxic nonprotein substance known,   in the case of the rough skinned newt. Many 
species also have eyesight that can sense into   the ultraviolet range, and have vision adapted 
to hunting at night, when they are carnivorous   opportunistic predators that are not restricted to 
consuming specific organisms, but organisms of a   specific size. Many species are territorial, 
and appear to be capable of biofluorescence.  In terms of diet, some, like the Japanese giant 
salamander, are large enough to eat crabs, small   mammals, and other amphibians. But most, like 
the dusky salamander, are much smaller and often   restricted to eating small to medium sized insects 
and annelids. Speaking of the dusky salamander,   a native to North America, salamander diversity 
is highest in the temperate regions, directly   contrary to the caecilians. Globally, their 
highest diversity anywhere is in North America   and specifically the Appalachian Mountains, where 
some species, such as the Shenandoah salamander,   are critically endangered, known to 
inhabit just three mountain peaks.  In terms of classification, the extant caudatans 
are often split into three suborders. Suborder   Cryptobranchoidea includes the hellbenders, 
Japanese giant salamander, South China Giant   salamander, and the Asiatic salamanders such 
as the Hida salamander. Suborder Sirenoidea   includes just a few species of sirens, all of 
which exhibit neoteny, meaning they maintain   their juveline forms as adults, and have only 
a tiny set of forelimbs without any hindlimbs.   Finally members of suborder Salamandroidea 
are the most biodiverse of all salamanders,   and often referred to as the advanced 
salamanders, including the mole salamanders,   such as the marbled salamander, the axolotl, 
and the Amphiumas, which are aquatic forms that   are sometimes called “congo snakes” or “conger 
eels” even though they are not closely related to   snakes or eels, or even the caecilians, though 
they somewhat resemble them morphologically.  Other significant members of this suborder include 
the lungless salamanders of Plethodontidae,   which can be extraordinarily locally abundant in 
Eastern North America. For example, an estimated   1.88 billion individuals of the southern redback 
salamander alone were found to inhabit just one   district of Mark Twain National Forest, providing 
a combined weight of 1,400 tons. Along with the   lungless plethodontids, the olms, mudpuppies, 
and torrent salamanders are also members of   order Salamandroidea, along with the true 
salamanders and newts of family Salamandridae,   sometimes referred to as the Salamandrids. 
The newts are contained within a subfamily of   Salamandridae known as Pleurodelinae, and are 
unique in that they alternate between aquatic   and terrestrial habitats with an additional 
juvenile form known as an eft, which looks like   a sexually mature form of an adult salamander 
but is not capable of reproduction. However,   their development can actually be even more 
complex. Larval forms of the eastern red newt   can become terrestrial “red efts” that may take 
from 2-8 years to mature into adults, or they   can directly become semi-aquatic adults, or even 
paedomorphs that retain larval characteristics but   can reproduce. Exactly which path the larval form 
takes depends on environmental factors. And with   that, we’ve covered two of the three orders of the 
class Amphibia. However, that still leaves over   7,000 species to cover, those of the order Anura. 
So let’s move forward and examine the frogs next.

tutorial, we also discussed an incident in which   the polymerization using the titanium-aluminum 
catalytic system did not work at all, as the   reaction stopped at an oligomerization stage, 
forming alpha-olefin products like 1-butene,   1-hexene, and higher homologs. The problem was 
attributed to trace contamination of nickel   metal. Once nickel was removed, 
the polymerization worked again.  This implies an early termination by 
beta-elimination of an M-H species, carried out   by the nickel contaminant. You may have wondered 
whether oligomerization of ethylene could also be   a useful process, given that lower alpha-olefins 
are not abundant in nature. The process would look   like this, for the dimerization of ethylene, where 
the metal M is still to be defined. As we can see,   an M-H species would undergo coordination 
of ethylene, followed by hydrometalation,   or addition of the M-H species to ethylene. 
Further ethylene coordination should be followed   by carbometalation, or insertion of the M-C bond 
across the ethylene double bond. This insertion   of ethylene into the growing alkyl chain can be 
repeated many times, and at some point termination   occurs by beta-elimination, regenerating the 
M-H catalyst and forming the alpha-olefin.  The oligomerization of ethylene using nickel 
catalysts has indeed become a reaction of great   importance. Every year, over one million tons of 
alpha-olefins are produced by what is known as   the SHOP process, which was first discovered in 
1968 at the Shell research group in Emeryville,   California. It was commercialized in 1977. In the 
1960s, Shell and other chemical companies searched   for an efficient process to prepare long-chain 
alpha-olefins, in the range C12-C18, which   were substrates for hydroformylation, leading to 
detergents, which need to have long enough chains   to form micelles. Hydroformylation is a process we 
introduced earlier in this series, so go back to   that tutorial if you need to refresh your memory.
The Shell group drew inspiration from the   Ziegler-Natta process and endeavored to find a 
homogeneous nickel catalyst which would lead to   long-chain terminal olefins. After screening 
many ligands and a Ni(0) source, they hit the   jackpot with alpha-diphenylphosphinoacetic 
acid. The catalyst was formed by interaction   of Ni-bis-cyclooctadiene, or Ni(COD)2 
and alpha-diphenylphosphinoacetic acid.   This produced alpha olefins with what is called 
a Flory-Schulz distribution. 1-butene, 1-hexene,   and 1-octene were major products, with 
the desired fraction C12-C18 constituting   about 40% of the entire mixture. Distillation 
afforded the desired fraction in modest yield.  For the process to be effective, the yield 
of the desired fraction had to be improved,   and therefore the SHOP process includes 
two extra steps to re-utilize the low and   high-molecular weight fractions. The second 
step is a heterogeneous catalytic step over   an aluminum catalyst at high temperature to 
bring about isomerization of the terminal   olefins to internal olefins. For example, 1-octene 
is isomerized to a mixture rich in 4-octene.  The final step is an olefin metathesis reaction 
using a heterogeneous catalyst based on   molybdenum. This combines long and short olefins 
to produced olefins of an intermediate length. For   example, 4-octene with 8 carbons, and 10-eicocene 
with 20 carbons, combine to form two molecules   of 1-tetradecene with 14 carbons, which is the 
desired length for the hydroformylation reaction.   At each pass of isomerization and metathesis, 
10-15% of the unwanted fractions are converted   to useful products, rendering the process more 
efficient. We will deal with metathesis reaction   later in the series. It was also found that using 
a polar solvent for the reaction, 1,4-butanediol,   the olefin products were immiscible and 
floated on the solvent layer containing the   catalyst. This made separation of the product 
trivial and recycling of the catalyst easy,   achieving excellent turnover numbers.
The mechanism of the reaction was   elucidated by German chemist Wilhelm Keim, who 
had been part of the Shell team, and in 1973   had returned to Germany to take a professorship 
at RWTH in Aachen, Germany. The catalyst itself   is formed from the precatalyst Ni(COD)2 
and phosphine in the presence of ethylene.   The Ni(0) species coordinates to the strong 
ligand, the phosphine, which expels one molecule   of COD from the coordination sphere of nickel. The 
next step can be seen as an oxidative addition of   the O-H bond of the ligand to the Ni(0) species, 
resulting in an oxidation of Ni(0) to Ni(II), the   active oxidation state. In the presence of COD, 
the Ni(II) catalyst can undergo hydrometalation   with COD to produce off-cycle species A, which 
is not productive and is at equilibrium with   the active Ni-H species. This can undergo 
fast ethylene hydrometalation and successive   carbometalations as we discussed. The timing 
of the beta-elimination depends on the reaction   conditions and can be fine-tuned to some extent.
The SHOP process is still being researched and   newer ligands sought in order to obtain a 
more narrow distribution. More recently,   chromium catalysts have been discovered at 
Chevron which produce 1-hexene or 1-octene in   over 70% selectivity. This has been the result of 
extensive metal and ligand screening. We will not   discuss these developments in detail, except to 
note that the mechanism is not identical to the   one we just described and therefore represents 
a special topic. The chemical company SASOL has   commercialized its 1-octene process to hundreds of 
thousands of tons of production per year. Overall,   about one million tons of 1-octene are produced 
each year by tetramerization of ethylene,   which is largely used as co-monomers in the 
Ziegler-Natta polymerization of ethylene,   leading to new plastic materials. Current 
intensive research in the ethylene oligomerization   area revolves around improving selectivities 
in alpha-olefin production, and given the   industrial importance of the olefin products, 
one can be sure of continuous breakthroughs.

## 11. Physical and Chemical Methods of Fingerprint Detection
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 5K | **Date:** 2 weeks ago | **Duration:** 8:28 | **ID:** rFk6tQlkh0o
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=rFk6tQlkh0o

### Transcript:
Say you walk into a crime scene. Maybe it’s a 
trashed apartment, a stolen car ditched in an   alley, or some creepy abandoned house straight 
out of a horror movie. You know the culprit   touched something: a door handle, a glass, maybe 
even a body. But you can’t see the fingerprints.   That’s the thing about fingerprints. They’re 
always there, practically mocking you in their   invisibility, until you bring out the right tools. 
If criminals were kind enough to dip their fingers   in paint before committing crimes, forensic 
work would be a breeze. But since they don’t,   science has to step in. Finding fingerprints 
isn’t some magical ability, it’s a process.   And before you even think about powders, fuming, 
or chemicals, you need to answer one question:   what kind of surface are we dealing with? The 
type of surface changes everything. Fingerprints   don’t behave the same way on glass as they do 
on paper, just like spilling coffee on a napkin   doesn’t look the same as spilling it on a table. 
That’s why forensic experts divide surfaces into   two main types, porous and non-porous. Porous 
surfaces are the real troublemakers. Paper,   cardboard, fabric, untreated wood, these soak 
up fingerprint residue like a sponge. The oils,   sweat, and amino acids left behind by a 
fingertip don’t just sit on top, they seep in,   becoming part of the material itself. That means 
regular powder won’t work here. Instead, we need   chemical reactions to make the prints appear. 
More on that in a moment. Non-porous surfaces,   on the other hand, are the easy ones. Smooth 
surfaces like glass, plastic, polished metal,   and ceramic don’t absorb fingerprint 
residue. Everything just sits there,   waiting to be found. Powders work well here, 
and if we want something more permanent,   chemical fuming seals the deal. And then we 
have the wild cards, the semi-porous surfaces,   such as leather, wax paper, and certain painted 
surfaces. They don’t fully absorb prints, but they   don’t keep them sitting on top either. These are 
unpredictable, and getting prints off them might   require a combination of different techniques.
Alright, so we’ve got our surfaces figured out.   Now let’s actually make these fingerprints show 
up. The first thing crime scene investigators   try isn’t powder or chemicals. It’s light. 
Alternate Light Sources, or ALS, use UV, infrared,   or laser-based lights to scan surfaces for 
hidden prints. Some substances in fingerprints,   like sweat, oil, and salt glow under certain 
wavelengths. If a fingerprint lights up under UV,   that’s great. No need for chemicals, and no risk 
of damaging evidence. But if nothing shows up,   it’s time to bring in the real tools. For 
non-porous surfaces, fingerprint powders are   the easiest and most common method. The principle 
here is adhesion. The fine particles in the powder   stick to the sweat and oils left behind by 
the fingerprint ridges. The better the ridges,   the better the adhesion, making the print visible. 
Black powder is the way to go. It’s made of carbon   or charcoal and stands out well on light-colored 
surfaces. Similarly, for a dark colored surface,   a light-colored powder is used for enhancing 
the contrast. If we’re dealing with something   delicate, though, magnetic powder is 
the way to go. Instead of using a brush,   forensic experts apply it with a magnetic 
wand, reducing the risk of smudging. And   for those annoying multicolored or patterned 
surfaces, fluorescent powder saves the day. It   glows under UV light, making the fingerprint 
pop even when the background is distracting.  But sometimes, powders just aren’t 
enough. Maybe the print is too faint,   or we need to preserve it for longer. That’s where 
superglue fuming, such as cyanoacrylate fuming,   comes in. This works on the simple principle 
of polymerization. When heated, the fumes from   superglue react with fingerprint residue and 
form a hard, white polymer coating over the   ridges. The print is now locked in place, meaning 
it won’t smudge or fade easily. Since this method   works great on non-porous surfaces like glass, 
plastic, and metal, it’s a favorite for crime   scene investigators handling objects that might 
be moved around or exposed to the elements. The   developed fingerprint impressions are lifted using 
tape at the end and subsequently photographed.  Now, what if we’re dealing with a porous 
surface? Powders are useless here because   the print is already inside the material. We need 
chemicals that react with fingerprint components   and drag them into visibility. Ninhydrin is the 
best candidate for this job. Originally used for   qualitative analysis of proteins, ninhydrin reacts 
with amino acids in sweat, turning prints into a   lovely shade of purple-blue, called Ruhemann’s 
purple, named after the scientist who discovered   ninhydrin. The reaction takes a while, but 
a little heat speeds things up. If you’ve   ever seen forensic scientists proudly holding up a 
piece of paper with a bunch of purple fingerprints   on it, that’s ninhydrin doing its job. For 
something even more sensitive, there’s DFO,   or 1,8-diazafluoren-9-one. This also reacts with 
amino acids, but with a interesting twist. It   fluoresces under UV light. That makes it easier 
to spot faint prints and capture them clearly.   More contrast means better visibility. And then 
we have silver nitrate, the last resort. This   works by a different principle, precipitation. 
It reacts with sodium chloride salt in sweat,   forming silver chloride. When exposed to 
light, silver chloride darkens, revealing the   fingerprint. The catch is that silver nitrate 
permanently alters the fingerprint residue,   meaning there’s no second chance. If you mess 
up the exposure, the print is gone forever.   That’s why this technique is a last resort.
There’s one other method that can be considered   as fitting under both physical and chemical 
categories. It works through sublimation,   like iodine fuming. Iodine crystals, when heated, 
turn straight into gas. These gas vapors then   adsorb on the fingerprint residue, temporarily 
revealing prints in a brownish shade. The downside   is that the prints fade fast. If you don’t fix 
them with a starch solution or benzoflavone,   or snap a quick photo, they’re gone. Because 
this involves fixation through a chemical   reaction with iodine, it can also be regarded as 
a chemical approach. Though less popular nowadays,   it is held in high regard due to its 
simplicity and cost-effectiveness.  Fingerprint detection isn’t just about randomly 
picking a method and hoping for the best.   It’s about understanding the science behind it, 
whether it’s adhesion, polymerization, amino acid   reactions, or salt precipitation. Everything 
depends on the surface. Smooth, non-porous   surface? Powders and superglue fuming. Porous 
surface? Ninhydrin and DFO. A standard protocol   involving sequential processing is conducted 
in fingerprint development, in which the least   invasive method is done first, followed by the 
more invasive methods. Remember, the fingerprint   is not the sole evidence out there. The object 
on which the fingerprint is deposited is itself   a piece of evidence. Sequential processing 
ensures that the substrates are not destroyed.   Reversibility, substrate sensitivity, and risk 
of overdevelopment are the three main pillars of   sequential processing. Let’s consider alternative 
light sources, iodine fuming, and ninhydrin. What   should be the correct order? The first should 
be obvious. ALS, which is non-invasive. Second,   iodine fuming, as it is a reversible reaction, 
given that it fades. Last would be ninhydrin   because it permanently alters the fingerprint.
There are even stranger techniques out there,   such as vacuum metal deposition, specialized 
chemical treatments, and methods that can recover   fingerprints from materials you’d never expect. 
However, whatever the development method is,   it ends up in photography, followed by enhancement 
of the photographs to visualize as many ridge   characteristics from the image as possible. For 
now, just take a look at the objects around you.   Every table, phone, and water bottle is covered 
in your fingerprints. Try to use a paint brush   and see if you can develop a fingerprint on 
your phone screen by using talcum powder.   Then lift it using tape, capture a photo, and 
try playing with image enhancement to study   the ridge characteristics. Then let’s move 
on and learn about fingerprint development.

Getting back to learning about what it would be 
like to live in Ancient Rome, imagine being a   student, or discipulus-ī, in ancient Rome. 
You would be going to school - schola-ae,   just like students do today. Curiously enough, 
the word for school could also be lūdus-i,   a word which in Latin means game or play.
There you would find your teacher - magister-trī.   He would teach you the basics in history 
- historia-ae, math - mathēmatica-ae,   literature - litterae-ārum and if you were a 
little older, even philosophy - philosophia-ae.  You would be sitting on your wooden desk - 
subsellium-iī. You would write on a tablet -   tabula-ae covered with wax - cēra-ae, using a pen 
or stylus - stilus-stilī. This instrument would   be pointed on one side to make incisions on the 
wax and flat on the other, to erase mistakes. The   tablet could be used again and again by warming up 
the wax to create a new clean surface, hence the   common expression tabula rasa meaning clean slate.
You would also use books - liber-rī. They were   written on some special paper made from papyrus 
- păpȳrus. The instrument for writing on this   surface was practically a reed, a calamus 
scriptōrius, cut at an angle and sharpened   like a quill by means of a special instrument - 
scalprum librārium. The reed was dipped into dark   ink - ātrāmentum-ī. When not in use, the calamus 
was stored in a small box called thēca calamāria.   For math you would be using a ruler - rēgula-ae 
and a counting board - abacus-ī. The teacher would   often use rolled books - volūmen-inis which were 
precisely stored in a shelf called librārium-iī.  You may be thinking, was life all work and no 
play for Roman children? Was there any time for   fun? There certainly was. Roman children 
would spend the day swimming - natō-āre,   singing - canō-ere, dancing - saltō-āre, riding 
horses - equitō-equitāre, hunting - vēnor-ārī,   fishing - piscor-ārī, and practicing in the gym 
- palaestra-ae. Ancient Romans also played a wide   variety of board games, including dice, using 
tessera-ae or ālea-ae, knucklebones - tālus- ī,   Roman Chess - lātrunculī-ōrum, Roman Checkers 
- calculī-ōrum, and ternī lapillī, which was   something called three pebbles, a strategy game 
that was sort of like tic-tac-toe. And with that,   we have a better sense of what it was like 
to be a young student in Ancient Rome.

Basically this is where we look at how the immune system and the nervous system interact with each other and influence each other's activity in the body. Since I work in a neuroimmunology lab, I'm also interested in the immune response during the experiment. We’ve spent quite a few tutorials learning 
about the societies, cultures, and politics   of the ancient world. Now let’s turn to the period 
that is generally considered to be the immediate   successor, the Middle Ages. The term “Middle Ages” 
was invented in early modern times to describe the   period between the 5th or 6th centuries CE, 
after the ancient world had come to an end,   and the Renaissance or “rebirth” of the 
13th through 15th centuries, which is seen   as a revival of the artistic, scientific, and 
philosophical achievements of the distant past,   as well as the first stirrings of the modern 
world. Strictly speaking, the idea of a   medieval period applies to the Mediterranean 
region and the European and African countries   that border it, but we will see that during 
those same centuries, there were changes and   developments in other parts of the world that 
are no less worth describing and discussing.  In the Mediterranean region itself, the 
geographical, cultural, and economic unity   that had characterized much of the history of the 
Roman Empire, gave way to a more decentralized and   fragmented world, as Huns, Goths, and other 
Germanic tribes invaded and settled in the   Empire’s western half. After centuries of turmoil, 
a center of political authority emerged in what   are now France and Germany, which became the heart 
of what was called the Holy Roman Empire, and   though this empire existed in one form or another 
for 1000 years, Europe was divided throughout   the Middle Ages into many states of varying sizes 
that were ruled by kings, princes, and dukes. The   eastern half of the Roman Empire, on the other 
hand, continued on as a political and cultural   unity in the form of the Byzantine Empire.
There were other large empires further to   the east, as the Arab conquests of the 7th 
and 8th centuries absorbed the Middle East,   Mesopotamia, and North Africa. These regions were 
united under governments called caliphates, and   they adopted the Muslim religion, language, and 
culture of their new rulers. A number of states   also arose on the Indian subcontinent. Starting 
in the 6th century CE, there was a period of   time during which India was divided into a 
series of small Hindu or Buddhist kingdoms,   but these came to an end in the 13th century, 
when a series of Muslim states called the Delhi   Sultanate ruled much of India for over 300 years. 
At the same time, a large swath of territory in   central Asia was conquered and governed by a 
mixture of ethnic groups known as Mongols. The   most extensive of their states were the Chinese 
empire of Genghis Khan, in the 13th century,   and the dynasty of Timur which followed it. 
Between the 7th and the 17th centuries, China   was primarily organized by a series of states 
ruled by native dynasties, which varied in their   size and power. Another unified east Asian state 
appeared in Japan, though the power of its emperor   waxed and waned, as local nobles took control of 
their own regions, and a shogun class, backed by   samurai, became the power behind the throne. In 
other parts of the medieval world, a number of   large and powerful states based on trade arose in 
various parts of sub-Saharan Africa during the 1st   millennium CE. The middle of the millennium was 
also a time when two large and powerful empires   appeared in central and South America, the Inca 
empire in Peru and the Aztec empire in Mexico,   well after the collapse of the Maya.
The Middle Ages are often described,   for better or for worse, as an “Age of Faith”. 
While the ancient world contained a wide variety   of religious practices and doctrines, which meant 
that, generally speaking, no one religious group   was privileged over the others, the medieval 
period was dominated by a few powerful faiths   which tended to suppress any religious movements 
or efforts at reform that might challenge them.   Both the Catholic authorities of the West, 
and the Orthodox authorities of the East,   launched frequent attacks, both rhetorical and 
actual, against any communities and doctrines that   they came to define as heretical. Additionally, 
the western and eastern churches fought and   competed with each other, until a permanent 
schism arose between them. Islam was divided   almost from the start between its Sunni and Shia 
communities. At the same time, Christians and   Muslims were engaged in a battle of cultures and 
ideologies. The two groups fought each other for   territorial supremacy in the Middle East, and at 
the borders that separated their two worlds. There   was still more conflict within Europe itself 
between the institutions of church and state,   as kings sought to control the churches in their 
territories, and popes entered into the world of   international politics. On the other hand, the 
church played a part in the creation of a European   culture, as it preserved the Latin language 
and aspects of classical civilization, and   supported literacy and learning throughout western 
Europe and its outlying regions. At the forefront   of this process were the monks of Ireland.
The transition from the Roman Empire to the world   of medieval Europe was, broadly speaking, one 
of decentralization and simplification, as large   cities gave way to smaller communities; economies 
became more local; trade went from transferring   money to bartering goods; and traveling from one 
place to another became rarer and more dangerous.   Large farms, which had once supplied even distant 
parts of the Empire, developed into independent   estates which produced most of their own goods; 
and farmers became serfs, who were bound to the   lord who owned the land where they were born. But 
during the same period, the Muslim world and China   were often organized into larger states which had 
sophisticated systems of trade and administration,   and were centers of cultural, scientific, and 
technological development. Their accomplishments   may have something to do with the fact that 
the soldiers who founded the Muslim caliphates,   and the administrators who governed them, were 
Arabs who were unified by a common ideology,   and a culture that encouraged philosophical 
and scientific inquiry, while China was an   ancient society with established traditions and a 
well-developed bureaucracy. For much of the Middle   Ages, the political, cultural and economic changes 
which took place in each region of the world,   Europe, China, Africa, and so on, had relatively 
little effect on the others. But with the spread   of exploration and trade, and the rise of national 
identities like “English” and “French”, this began   to change. Though it was often destructive and 
tragic, the increasing contact between the old   and new worlds, and between the global north and 
south, helped to bring about the more intertwined   and interdependent world we know today.
Since the concept of a medieval period best   fits the history of Western Europe, we’ll start 
there, with the kingdoms of Charlemagne and his   successors; the beginnings of the nations we know 
today; their interactions with the Muslim world;   and the far- reaching consequences of the Black 
Death. We’ll then move on to the Byzantine Empire,   and the states that were at various times its 
allies and enemies, such as Hungary, Bulgaria,   and Ukraine. After that, we’ll look at the role 
of the Vikings in the politics and wars of both   eastern and western Europe. We’ll then turn to the 
series of states which made up the Muslim world;   and to the Mongol empires, or khanates, of central 
Asia. Then we’ll move farther east, to the many   states of India; the dynasties of medieval China; 
and the series of eras into which Japanese history   is traditionally divided. Finally, we’ll look 
at the some of the large African empires,   both before and after they came into contact with 
the seafaring nations of Europe; and the complex   civilizations of Mesoamerica. So let’s move 
forward and start learning about the Middle Ages.

acid quench. Although the reaction was not clean,   also producing resins and terminal olefins, 
Ziegler recognized the potential of alkylmetal   compounds to undergo sequential carbometalation 
and potentially lead to useful polymers.  Moving to other main-group metals, Ziegler focused 
his attention on trialkylaluminum compounds,   which are extremely pyrophoric compounds, 
meaning they ignite spontaneously when exposed   to air. This is because the carbon-aluminum bond 
readily oxidizes in the presence of oxygen gas.   It was found that triethylaluminum in hydrocarbon 
solvents adds readily to ethylene under pressure   at 100oC to yield high molecular weight trialkyl 
aluminum compounds. These, upon oxidation,   yielded a statistical mixture of long-chain 
aliphatic alcohols, which find use as active   ingredients in detergents and other products.
The result was rather surprising, because   trialkylaluminum compounds, usually prepared in 
ether solvents, were considered quite inert to   carbometalation reactions. The explanation is that 
trialkylaluminum reagents are strong Lewis acids,   and they form a tight complex with 
ethers, which are very good Lewis bases,   and these complexes are quite unreactive. Working 
instead in hydrocarbon solvents unmasked new   reactivity patterns for these compounds.
At this point, a fortuitous failure led   to a key development. One day the polymerization 
reaction failed, and instead yielded 1-butene gas,   obtained by an apparent beta-elimination of an 
aluminum hydride. The troubleshooting analysis   indicated that traces of nickel in the autoclave 
may have been responsible for the anomalous   result, meaning that traces of a nickel catalyst 
promoted a new beta-elimination reaction. This was   indeed confirmed experimentally. In the 1950s, the 
chemistry of transition metals was in its infancy,   and their catalytic properties were 
just beginning to be discovered.  The reasoning was that perhaps one could find a 
transition metal compound which could catalyze   the polymerization reaction. The experiment using 
catalytic amounts of titanium tetrachloride with   triethylaluminum hit the jackpot. Polymerization 
rates were improved by many orders of magnitude,   and polymers with molecular weights of up to 
3,000,000 were obtained at room temperature!   These were the first samples of modern PE plastic.
Naturally, Ziegler decided to patent the   invention. In the meantime, a licensing agreement 
had been signed with the Italian petroleum company   Montecatini and their consultant, Professor Natta. 
Natta and Montecatini extended the polymerization   to polypropylene, another plastic which turned out 
to have immense commercial potential, and changed   the catalyst from TiCl4 to TiCl3, which made 
the chemistry more effective. At the same time,   other companies were experimenting with similar 
chemistry and a huge patent battle ensued for the   rights to the chemistry. It was a legal battle 
without precedent, which lasted decades. Only in   1982, long after Professor Ziegler’s death, 
did the Max Planck Institute win the battle   and was awarded damages from companies deemed to 
be violating MPI’s intellectual property rights.  Over the last 60 years, the search for new 
catalysts has been intense, and there are now   dozens of effective catalysts based on a number of 
transition metals. The mechanism has been studied   using titanium and zirconium cyclopentadienyl 
complexes, which are homogeneous systems which   facilitate the reaction. In a simplified 
scheme, the metal-chlorine bond of the   catalyst is replaced, via the aluminum reagent, 
to yield a metal-alkyl bond, and these species   are converted in situ to cationic titanium 
or zirconium alkyls, which insert ethylene   or propylene at a rate many orders of magnitude 
faster than the carbon-aluminum bond of aluminum   compounds. Termination is a complex process which 
is carefully controlled. It can be spontaneous,   such as by beta-hydride elimination, 
or induced, with hydrogen gas or acids.  Of course, chemists have extended 
this process to other olefins,   and even mixtures of olefins, giving rise to 
new polymers and co-polymers. In addition,   catalyst development is still a fertile area of 
research and new systems continue to be developed,   patented, and implemented on scale. In general, 
however, it was the serendipitous discovery by   Ziegler that transition metal-alkyl reagents can 
polymerize olefins very efficiently which opened   a fertile new area of research, leading not only 
to a host of publications and mechanistic studies,   but also to important commercial products. As 
often occurs, the scientific breakthrough was   triggered by an unexpected result, and this 
highlights the value of the famous dictum:   luck favors the prepared mind. Ziegler 
did not overlook an anomalous result, but   investigated it and capitalized on it, achieving 
a scientific breakthrough worthy of a Nobel prize.

Imagine a huge reference library with lots 
of books. They are sorted according to the   subjects. There are lots of subjects and lots 
of topics within a subject. Searching for a   book on a particular topic within this library 
would be a tedious task. What if there was a   further sub-classification based on the author’s 
name, or division into different sub-topics?   Retrieval of a particular book would be a lot 
easier. Similarly, fingerprints need to be   classified systematically to make the process of 
identification easier. In this tutorial, we will   try to understand how Henry’s classification 
of fingerprints works. As we learned when   discussing the history of fingerprints, they were 
first officially used for identification in the   Bengal province of India by Sir William Herschel. 
However, fingerprints were still not assimilated   as a means of identification in criminal matters.
The police used to rely on anthropometry,   which involved observing and documenting 
bodily features and physical measurements   for identification. This was despite anthropometry 
having its list of disadvantages and limitations,   such as two individuals sharing a common set 
of physical features. But it was the consensus   back then that there exists no better technique 
than anthropometry for criminal identification.   This was when Sir Edward Henry was impressed by 
the obvious merits of fingerprints and started   toying with the idea of using fingerprints either 
in addition to or instead of anthropometry. He   discussed this proposal extensively with pioneers 
of fingerprint science such as Sir Francis Galton.   Henry realized that the current system of 
fingerprint classification was based only on   their pattern types. There existed no method that 
sorted fingerprints in a scientific yet simple   manner that would permit easy retrieval and rapid 
identification of a person whose fingerprints   have already been recorded. This was one of the 
reasons why fingerprints were not inculcated into   law enforcement. So, Henry, with his subordinates, 
sub-inspectors Azizul Haque and Hemchandra Bose,   worked extensively from 1896 to 1897 to develop a 
standard fingerprint classification system. It was   Azizul Haque who proposed a mathematical formula 
to supplement Henry’s idea of classification. The   original classification system, as proposed by 
Henry, took into consideration all the fingers   and converted the patterns present on them into 
the form of letters and numbers that could be   easily arranged in the form of a fraction. Now 
that we are familiar with the background behind   this system, let us understand it in detail.
Henry’s original system of classification   involves four main divisions: primary, secondary, 
sub-secondary, and final. Let's go through them   one at a time. The first stage of classification 
is the primary classification. It is a ten-finger   classification, which essentially means that 
all of the fingerprints from both hands are   studied here. This fingerprint card is known as a 
ten-print card. Let’s look at how the fingers are   numbered on this card. Hold both of your hands in 
such a way that the palm of your right-hand faces   you while the palm of your left-hand faces the 
opposite direction. Start counting your fingers   from the right thumb to the left little finger. 
This is the order in which fingerprints are   numbered on a fingerprint card. The right hand is 
numbered 1-5 and the left hand is numbered 6-10,   from thumb to little finger. The primary division 
of classification is also known as the whorl   division. As the name implies, this system only 
considers the whorl patterns present on your   fingers. Each finger is assigned a numerical 
value, and that value is given to the finger   only when a whorl pattern is present on it. Here, 
the term whorl pattern includes all the variants,   such as accidental, central pocket, and a double 
loop. If a finger has an arch or a loop pattern,   the value given to that finger is zero. The 
values assigned to the fingers are simple,   as shown in this table. Starting from 
the right thumb: 16-16, 8-8, 4-4, 2-2,   1-1. As you can see, the value halves after 
every two fingers. Easy to remember, right?  Adding up the values for even-numbered fingers, 
(2, 4, 6, 8, 10) generates a numerator;   odd-numbered fingers, (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) form the 
denominator. So the lowest possible value for   primary classification will be 0/0. Right? 
Actually that’s wrong. To avoid confusion   between the numeral "0" and the letter "O", which 
is used in ridge tracing to denote an outer whorl,   1 is added to both sums. So 1/1 becomes the 
lowest value and 32/32 will be the highest   value when all fingerprints are whorls. Azizul 
Haque, Henry’s colleague, discovered a method   to group a set of fingerprints in 1024 pigeon 
holes according to primary classification. This   setup was designed in such a way that there were 
32 rows, with each row having 32 pigeon holes.   Primary classification, though it technically 
generates 1,024 combinations, or 32 times 32,   practical limitations arise. Over 25% of people 
fall into the 1/1 category due to whorl scarcity,   underscoring the need for deeper classification.
Secondary Classification simplifies things by   encoding patterns on the index fingers. The 
right index, finger 2, dictates the numerator,   and the left index, finger 7, dictates 
the denominator. Patterns are labeled:   A (plain arch), T (tented arch), W (whorl), U 
(ulnar loop), or R (radial loop). For example,   U/U denotes ulnar loops on both index fingers.
Next, Sub-Secondary Classification looks at index,   middle, and ring fingers. Whorls undergo ridge 
tracing to determine if they’re inner (I),   outer (O), or meeting (M), based on ridges between 
the traced line and right delta. Loops, meanwhile,   are classified via ridge counts: index loops with 
less than or equal to 9 ridges are inner (I),   greater than 9 are outer (O); middle loops use 
less than or equal to 10 (I) vs. greater than   10 (O); ring loops follow less than or equal 
to 13 (I) vs. greater than 13 (O). Results   from the right and left hands form a fraction 
such as IIM/IIO, thereby adding granularity.  Then, Final Classification prioritizes the little 
fingers. If the right little finger is a loop,   its ridge count defines the final value. If not, 
the left little finger is checked. For whorls,   an “ulnar loop” is simulated by counting ridges 
between the core and left delta. In practice, only   one value is recorded. For example, a right little 
loop with 12 ridges yields a final classification   of 12. This is how the classification is 
represented altogether. Primary, Secondary,   Sub-secondary, and Final. The line present in 
between the numerators and denominators is known   as the classification line. Barring the primary 
classification, where even-numbered fingers   form the numerator and odd-numbered fingers form 
the denominator, the rest of the divisions have   right-handed fingers as numerators and left-handed 
fingers as denominators. Two additional divisions   were added later, known as Key and Major. Though 
being the latest to be discovered, these divisions   are always represented before the Primary 
classification so as not to disrupt the original   order. The Key is the ridge count of the first 
non-little-finger loop, let’s say 11 for a right   index loop, and appears above the classification 
line. The Major analyzes thumbs. Whorls undergo   ridge tracing, for example 3 ridges equals inner, 
while loops use ridge counts. Values for both   thumbs, right above and left below, are noted.
While Henry’s system revolutionized   fingerprinting, modern adaptations address its 
gaps. The FBI added subdivisions such as WCDX for   complex whorls and a “special loops” category. 
Digital systems now automate classification,   reducing manual errors inherent in analogue 
pigeonhole storage. Yet Henry’s core logic   endures: layered, hierarchical analysis 
that balances breadth and precision,   proving even century-old frameworks 
can evolve without losing relevance.

**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 4K | **Date:** 3 weeks ago | **Duration:** 11:08 | **ID:** 6pOW7dMReX8

In the previous tutorial, we covered the 
general characteristics and development   of amphibians. Now let’s dive into amphibian 
body systems, which include the integumentary,   skeletal, muscular, respiratory, circulatory, 
digestive, excretory, nervous, lymphatic,   reproductive, and endocrine systems.
An amphibian’s integumentary system is   comprised of their skin, which is often thin and 
moist, and is only loosely attached to the body at   certain points. It contains two layers, an outer 
stratified epidermis which is shed periodically,   and an inner spongy dermis. The skin is 
notable for containing deposits of keratin,   and more terrestrial amphibians such as toads 
have especially heavy deposits of keratin,   though amphibian keratin in general is soft, 
unlike the hardened keratin that forms the scales,   claws, horns, hair, and feathers of the amniotes. 
Without this hardened keratinized tissue,   an amphibian’s epidermis instead produces small 
mucosal glands that secrete a protective mucus,   which helps to waterproof the skin, and 
larger glands that produce a whitish,   watery poison which is irritating to predators. 
Although all amphibians produce a skin poison,   its effectiveness and degree of irritation varies 
wildly by species. For example, species of genus   Phyllobates, a small genus of poison arrow frogs, 
are renowned for their toxin. It’s worth noting   here though that this is a poison, which is 
different from a venom. A poison is a toxin   that is ingested or absorbed, while venom is a 
toxin that is injected through a bite or sting.  In addition to these glands, an amphibian’s 
coloration is visible due to chromatophores,   which in amphibians are branched cells that 
contain pigment and are often of three types:   First, xanthophores, which contain yellow, orange, 
or red pigments. Beneath these lie iridophores,   which contain a silver light reflecting 
pigment. And beneath those are the melanophores,   which contain black or brown melanin. Many of the 
brilliant colors of amphibians are produced by the   interaction of these pigments. The green color, 
for example, is produced due to an interaction   between the yellow pigmented xanthophores and the 
underlying iridophores that produce a blue color,   an example of Tyndall scattering. This 
blue light is filtered by the overlying   yellow pigment, so it appears to be green.
The endoskeleton is the cornerstone of the   amphibian skeletal system, and it is comprised of 
bone and cartilage that provides attachment points   for their muscular system. While some, like the 
salamanders, have long bodies and weaker limbs,   others, like the frogs, have a highly adapted 
musculoskeletal system that is specially adapted   for jumping and swimming through simultaneous 
extensor thrusts of the hindlimbs. In addition,   the skull of the anurans in particular differs 
greatly from other vertebrates, as it is   much lighter, less ossified, and flattened.
In terms of the amphibian respiratory system,   as adults, amphibians use three surfaces for 
respiratory gas exchange with the surrounding   air. Those are the skin, for cutaneous breathing, 
the mouth, for buccal breathing, and the lungs,   which function similarly to the lungs of other 
tetrapods, though they are often less developed   and sometimes entirely missing, like in the 
lungless salamanders. Even in species that   perform lung breathing, the majority of their 
carbon dioxide is lost directly across the skin.   In addition, the lungs of those who have them are 
often ovoid and divided into small terminal air   chambers called faveoli. Amphibians, and frogs 
in particular, are known as positive pressure   breathers that fill their lungs by forcing air 
into them. They do this by first lowering the   floor of the mouth, then drawing air in through 
the nostrils and opening the glottis, and forcing   air into the lungs by raising the floor of the 
mouth, then closing the glottis. They can then,   with air stored in the lungs, rhythmically 
move the mouth cavity and thus participate   in buccal breathing at the same time as they use 
their lungs and skin for enhanced gas exchange.  In addition, the respiratory system of vocalizing 
amphibians, namely frogs, contains vocal cords   that are located in the larynx that are 
often more developed in males than females.   They produce sound by passing air back and forth 
over the cords between the lungs and a large pair   of vocal sacs in the floor of the mouth, that 
are also used by males as effective resonators to   attract mates with unique sound patterns. Though 
frogs are without a doubt the loudest amphibians,   there are some salamanders, such as the California 
giant salamander, which have vocal cords and can   produce a barking sound, while caecilians have 
been recorded making a clicking sound underground.  The amphibian circulatory system is a closed 
system of arteries and veins that connect to   a vast network of capillaries, through which 
blood is pumped via the heart. Frog hearts   have two separate atria and a single undivided 
ventricle. Blood entering the heart from the body,   via the systemic circuit, first enters a 
large receiving chamber, the venous sinus,   and then the right atrium. Meanwhile, the left 
atrium receives freshly oxygenated blood from the   lungs and skin, via the pulmonary circuit. These 
two atria then contract asynchronously, meaning   at different times, and pump either oxygenated or 
deoxygenated blood into the ventricle. This means   that although there is a single ventricle the 
oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix,   and is kept separate by the spiral valve which 
divides the systemic and pulmonary flows.  In terms of the digestive system, all extant adult 
amphibians are carnivorous. Most are opportunistic   predators that will consume anything they can 
catch, and is small enough to swallow whole.   Since most amphibians are rather small, this 
means they prey mainly upon insects, spiders,   small annelids, snails, and other slow-moving 
invertebrates. However, some amphibians like the   American and African bullfrogs can get to be quite 
large and have been seen preying upon snakes,   lizards, rats, and even birds. Many of the most 
active predators snap at moving prey using their   protrusible tongue that attaches at the front 
of their mouth and is free at the posterior end,   which produces a sticky secretion that 
sticks to prey and pulls it into the mouth,   where numerous tiny teeth serve to grasp the prey 
but not to chew. The prey is then passed whole,   and usually living, into the esophagus, and then 
stomach where digestion begins. The remainder of   the digestive tract is relatively short, but 
they do possess a pancreas, liver, and gall   bladder. Their excretory system is comprised 
of two kidneys that serve to filter the blood.   It’s worth noting that the digestive system of 
larval forms is often quite different from adults.   Frog tadpoles for example are often thought of as 
herbivorous and possess long spiraled digestive   tracts. However, they will opportunistically 
feed on animal tissue if they can find it.  The amphibian nervous system is essentially 
the same as all vertebrates in that they have   a central brain, spinal cord, and nerves 
throughout the body. Though their brains   are often regarded as simple, many species 
have been found to show associative learning,   the ability to distinguish between high and 
low numbers, and have been widely regarded as   sentient. They are also, contrary to old myths, 
capable of feeling pain, like any vertebrate, and   potentially harbor a range of emotional states.
The semiterrestrial life of an amphibian marks   a departure from the purely aquatic life of their 
ancestors, though their links are still apparent.   For example, the pressure-sensitive lateral-line 
system of fish does exist in amphibians,   but only in their larval forms, and a few that 
are strictly aquatic as adults, like the axolotl,   though it looks a bit different than in 
fish. In terms of sensory structures,   vision is the primary sense in most amphibians, 
except the mostly blind caecilians. Many have   large and dominant eyes that are kept moist by 
lachrymal glands. They often include a large lens   and a retina that contains both rods and cones, 
a well-developed iris, and a nictitating membrane   that can move across the lower eye surface. 
Amphibians also have well-developed tactile   and chemical receptors in their skin, taste buds 
on the tongue and palate, and a well-developed   olfactory system. In addition, though some 
amphibians may be entirely deaf, ears are well   developed in frogs and contain a large tympanic 
membrane, or eardrum, that is externally visible   and contains a columella that transmits vibrations 
to the inner ear, which contains a utricle,   a saccule that bears a lagena, partly coverd by 
a tectorial membrane, which can sense different   sound frequencies that differ by species and 
aid in discerning calls during mating season.  The amphibian lymphatic system is characterized 
by large lymphatic sacs and two pairs of lymph   hearts that return lymph into the circulatory 
system. They typically lack lymph nodes,   and their lymphatic vessels are sparse or 
nonexistent. In addition, the spleen and   the mucous membrane lining the gut and respiratory 
tract serve as important immune system components.   Note that this is not the case for all 
amphibians, and the lymphatic system may   be entirely absent in some families, though 
it always seems to be present in anurans.  The amphibian reproductive system includes testes 
in males and ovaries in females. Reproduction is   often external in frogs, but often internal 
in caudatans and caecilians. Reproduction   often requires water and involves a metamorphic 
stage that is especially complex in anurans.  Finally, the amphibian endocrine system, 
as is typical in the vertebrates,   plays a crucial role in regulating various 
physiological processes, including growth,   metabolism, and reproduction. Key endocrine 
organs include the pituitary gland, thyroid   gland, and adrenal glands. The pituitary gland 
produces hormones that stimulate the thyroid and   adrenal glands, influencing metabolism 
and stress response. The thyroid gland   regulates metabolism and development, while 
the adrenal glands produce corticosteroids,   responding to stress. Additionally, the 
gonads, or testes and ovaries, release sex   hormones essential for reproduction. That about 
wraps up our survey of body systems, but there’s   still lots to learn about amphibians. So let’s 
move forward and examine their diversity next.
