We have made a lot of progress in examining 
phylum Chordata, having gotten through many   vertebrate clades, and we have now arrived at 
the tetrapods. The first tetrapod clade we will   examine is the amphibians, as they evolved first. 
The earliest amphibians evolved in the Devonian   period from the sarcopterygian fish with lungs and 
bony-limbed fins. Looking again at the cladogram,   we will notice that the amphibians are a sister 
clade to the amniotes, which includes all other   tetrapods. Amphibians, reptiles, birds, and 
mammals are all members of phylum Chordata,   they are also vertebrates, gnathostomes, meaning 
jawed, they are bony, and thus Osteichthyes,   they qualify as lobe-finned fish, or 
Sarcopterygii, are all members of Tetrapoda,   because their ancestors were four-limbed, and 
many of them also share this characteristic in   their present forms. Modern amphibians range in 
size from the 7.7 millimeter long microhylid frog,   Paedophryne amanuensis, that was discovered in 
2012, all the way up to the 1.8 meter or 5 feet 11   inches long South China giant salamander. In order 
to better study the amphibians we will split their   form and function into two tutorials. In this 
tutorial, we will go over their evolutionary   origins, general characteristics, basic phylogeny, 
reproduction and development, and conservation.  It is widely accepted that amphibians began to 
emerge and diversify about 370 million years   ago during the Devonian period. These early 
forms evolved from lobe-finned fish, marking   a transition from aquatic to terrestrial life for 
the chordate lineage. During the Carboniferous   period, a significant radiation occurred, giving 
rise to diverse amphibian forms and sizes. Notable   groups like labyrinthodonts showcased adaptations 
for both aquatic and terrestrial environments,   with limbs and digits facilitating terrestrial 
locomotion. During this time in the fossil record   we see a multitude of transitional forms such 
as Ichthyostega, which had four sturdy limbs,   a neck, a tail with fins, and a skull similar 
to that of the lobe-finned fish Eusthenopteron.   Though there is some debate as to which fossil 
forms are or aren’t amphibians, all extant forms   within the class Amphibia are also in the subclass 
Lissamphibia, meaning “smooth amphibians”,   which includes the Anurans, Caudatans, and 
Gymnophionans. The earliest fossils widely   attributed to these modern amphibians don’t 
show up until the Permian. This means that   for quite some time, the ancient amphibians were 
the dominant terrestrial chordates. Indeed some   of them, like Prionosuchus and Mastodonsaurus, 
were well over five meters in length. And although   they may look reptilian, they are actually only 
distantly related to the famous dinosaurs which   dominated the globe after the Permian extinction. 
However, although there are a great deal of   fascinating extinct amphibians from Beelzebufo 
to Gerrothorax, since this is a zoology series,   we’re going to focus on their extant forms.
Amphibians are the only tetrapods that are not   amniotes. That is, they do not produce amniotic 
eggs and instead produce yolky, or mesolecithal   eggs with jellylike membranes. Many go through 
a detailed period of metamorphosis from larval   to adult forms. And as adults, most of them are 
four-limbed, and those with limbs generally have   a forelimb with four digits and a hindlimb with 
five. They also have relatively lighter skulls   than most vertebrates, as well as skeletons which 
are often less ossified and primarily composed   of bone with varying numbers of vertebrae. They 
also lack true nails, and often have webbed feet,   in the case of the anurans. Most notably, 
amphibians also have smooth, moist, and glandular   skin modified for cutaneous respiration, meaning 
they can exchange gases through their skin without   lungs. In fact, an entire family, Plethodontidae, 
are known as “lungless salamanders”. They are   also noted for their pigment cells and 
glands that secrete defensive compounds.  As we mentioned, all extant amphibians are also 
in the subclass Lissamphibia. Order Gymnophiona   includes about 200 known species of legless 
caecilians, and order Caudata includes over   725 species of salamanders, which includes the 
newts, axolotls, and many others. However, the   diversity of these orders are dwarfed by Anura, 
which are commonly referred to as frogs, and   include over 7,500 species, or nearly 90% of all 
extant amphibians, making them the most biodiverse   and widespread of all modern amphibians.
Speaking of diversity, reproduction and   development varies by amphibian order. We 
typically think of amphibian development through   the lens of an anuran, where the males call to 
attract mates, females then choose a male and he   embraces her in a grasp known as amplexus, until 
she makes it to the water and lays eggs which he   fertilizes externally. These fertilized eggs, or 
zygotes, then begin developing almost immediately   and become a hollow ball of cells, or blastula, 
through repeated division, or cleavage, which   undergoes gastrulation and develops into an embryo 
with a tail bud. This is nourished by yolk until   it hatches 2 to 21 days later, as a tadpole with 
external gills that grows a skinfold over those   gills and begins its herbivorous or scavenging 
life. These tadpoles have a distinct head, trunk,   and tail, and develop into froglets by first 
growing their hind limbs followed by forelimbs,   and then absorb their tails, and completely 
rearrange their respiratory and digestive systems   for a semi or fully terrestrial life as adults. In 
some species this may take as little as 3 months   or less, and the young begin developing rapidly, 
while others, like the bullfrogs, may remain as   tadpoles and continue to grow in size for 2 to 
3 years or more before they begin metamorphosis.  Although this process is true for most 
temperate anurans, this story is not true   for all amphibians, or even of all anurans. For 
one, although most frogs show no parental care,   the South American pygmy marsupial frog, for 
example, carries their larvae in a dorsal pouch,   while male Darwin’s frogs carry their 
developing froglets in their vocal pouches,   and Surinam toads carry their fertilized eggs in 
embedded brooding pouches on their back. Others,   like those of genus Eleutherodactylus hatch from 
eggs as small frogs and bypass the tadpole stage   entirely. Meanwhile, a male caecilian fertilizes a 
female internally by way of his phallodeum, which   he inserts into the female’s cloaca. The eggs 
hatch as miniature versions of the parents which   then use their teeth to bite off pieces of their 
mothers nutritious mucus-covered skin, and consume   it along with secretions from her cloaca which 
they subsist on for weeks. Interestingly enough,   this skin contains dense nutrients for growth and 
development, much like the breast milk of mammals.  Many salamanders of order Caudata also engage in 
internal fertilization, where the male deposits   a spermatophore, which is a small packet of sperm, 
in the air or underwater. The female then takes up   the sperm packet by grasping it with the lips 
of the cloaca and pushing it into the vent.   The female may then carry the fertilized eggs for 
some time before depositing them in or near a body   of water, where at hatching the emerging larval 
form has eyes without lids, teeth in both upper   and lower jaws, three pairs of feathery external 
gills, and a long tail with dorsal and ventral   fins. The forelimbs may be partially developed 
and the hindlimbs are rudimentary in pond-living   species, but may be more developed in species that 
reproduce in moving water. Their metamorphosis   into adults is often less pronounced than in frogs 
because they already closely resemble the adults   and unlike tadpoles are already carnivorous. 
Some species, like the now famous axolotl,   remain in this juvenile form for their entire 
lives and sexually mature as juveniles,   a phenomenon known as pedomorphosis, while 
gilled adults are known as perennibranchiates,   though they can in rare conditions undergo 
metamorphosis. Meanwhile, lungless salamanders   of family Plethodontidae are terrestrial and lay 
a small number of unpigmented eggs in a cluster   among damp leaf litter. Each egg has a large yolk 
sac, and the larva feeds on this while it develops   inside the egg, and eventually emerges as a fully 
formed juvenile salamander. While they develop,   many females will often brood and defend 
these eggs against predators until they hatch.  In terms of conservation, more than a third 
of amphibians are currently threatened with   extinction. Their global decline has been 
recognized since the 1980s when the extinct golden   toad went from one of the most common species 
to completely extinct in a matter of years.   There are a number of threats that contribute 
to their decline, such as habitat destruction   and modification, over-exploitation, pollution, 
introduced and invasive species, global warming,   and especially diseases like chytridiomycosis 
which is caused by several species of chytrid   fungi that have been linked to massive 
declines in amphibian populations in North,   Central, and South America, Australia, 
East Africa and much of the Caribbean.  However, all is not lost for amphibians. There 
are numerous international efforts to save native   species, and release captive bred populations into 
the wild. Some, like the Panamanian Golden Frog,   may be entirely extinct in the wild though they 
thrive in captivity. Organizations like the   Smithsonian are working to breed disease resistant 
individuals and release them back to their native   lands. Though their future is unknown, at 
least the efforts to save them have increased   dramatically since their decline was noted. And 
with that we’ve covered a brief overview of the   amphibians and their conservation. Let’s move 
forward and check out their body systems next.

[singing] [music] ience. >> In the previous tutorial, we discussed the development and structure of the standard model. We talked about the three main groups of particles that make up the model. Quarks, lepttons, and bosons. We explored predictions that the standard model has made and how it has proven to be one of the most successful theories in the history of science. We also mentioned the shortcomings of the model and the exciting research that is ongoing to address these and improve it. Finally, we touched on the detection and acceleration methods used by experimental particle physicists to interact with these particles. However, to effectively measure particles and characterize their behavior, there must be a well- motivated place and time to look for them. This means that the lifetimes of particles and the chances of them interacting with each other are extremely important quantities. This tutorial will explore these concepts and ask the fundamental question, why do particles decay at all? The idea of particle decay is somewhat surprising. Why do all particles undergo some form of decay unless prevented from doing so by a conservation law? The simple answer is that these non-fundamental particles can be thought of as excitations, kind of like an electron that has been promoted to an excited state within an atom. Non-fundamental particles exist at a higher energy state than some combination of fundamental particles which makes them unstable. It is energetically favorable for these particles to decay down to the lower energy configuration of fundamental particles. So they do precisely that at a particular rate depending on their identity. Naturally, one would assume that this means many of the particles that exist in our universe today are fundamental. This is largely true. Electrons, photons, and nutrinos are among the most common. However, protons and neutrons are also very common. Even though they aren't fundamental particles, they are made up of quarks and gluons, and they have long lifetimes because of gluon bonds and nuclear stability. Interestingly, isolated protons do not decay, but isolated neutrons do. This disparity along with the lifetime of the neutron is the subject of ongoing research. Speaking of lifetimes, what is the lifetime of a particle and how can it be calculated? Lifetime does not refer to the exact number of seconds that it takes a given particle to decay. Rather, it refers to the average lifetime of the particles in a sample of them. This is dictated by the difference in energy between the particle and its decay products. We know from conservation of energy that on its own, a particle cannot decay into products that are at a higher combined energy than the original particle. However, even if the products are at a very slightly lower energy, the decay is theoretically possible and is simply a lot less likely to occur due to the small energy difference. Generally, the probability of a decay occurring is related to the energy difference between the initial and final states of the decay. The probability of a decay per unit time is called the decay rate gamma. The lifetime of a particle toao is then just one over gamma. And the number of particles at any given time can be written as n= n initial * e to the negative t over towo where n initial is the initial number of particles in the sample. For some particles, there are multiple fundamental particle configurations that can be decay products. In these cases, the decay with the largest energy difference is most likely to occur and the other possibilities occur with lower probabilities. The percentage of all decays with which each possibility occurs is called the branching ratio and each of these has a corresponding decay rate. The total decay rate can be found by adding together the individual decay rates and all the rest of the math can be done the same as before. Branching ratios and particles that can undergo multiple types of decay are extremely valuable experimental tools. the relative abundance of decay products can be observed and this can inform physicists about which initial particle was present. The other important quantity that needs to be discussed when talking about particle decay and interaction is the cross-section. The cross-section can be thought of as a target size for a particle interaction or scatter. It describes how much space there is for an incoming stream of particles to hit and is therefore a measure of how likely an interaction is with units of area that are called barns. Most cross-sections are on the order of millibarns 10 -3, but they can go all the way down to femtob barns 10 -15 or atob barns 1018. It isn't the same as a target though because as particles get closer to the target, they deflect more rather than a binary hit or miss. This is due to the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics and effects like quantum tunneling. Cross-section depends on a lot of different variables, including the velocity of the incident particles and the forces that mediate the interaction. This interaction is often a type of scattering. Scattering is the process by which particles interact and deflect from their original paths when they encounter other particles or forces. This reveals information about the structure and dynamics of the interaction. By studying particle scattering, physicists can probe the different forces and components that make up the standard model. For example, looking at electron proton scattering led to the discovery of quarks. Common types of scattering are responsible for many phenomena seen all around us including the color of the sky which is due to ray scattering. Scattering can take place with the deflection of a particle or it can involve multiple products that exit at different energies and angles. We can label theta as a scattering angle defined as the deflection angle between the incident particle and scattered particle. If we also define the cross-section as sigma and an impact parameter B that describes the distance from a scattering surface, most types of scattering problems can be solved. Another useful tool is the differential cross-section which is defined as d of theta equals the derivative of sigma with respect to omega which is also equal to b / s of theta* the derivative of b with respect to theta. Here d omega is a solid angle. This can be used to explore the scattering angle in more depth or explore the energy dependency of the cross-section. It is not a purely physical measurement but rather represents the probability of a scattering event occurring. Both the cross-section and decay rate are made up of two main factors. The amplitude of a process M and the phase space available or density of final states known as row. When finding these, Ferm's golden rule can be used. Ferm's golden rule essentially states that the decay rate and cross-section are both proportional to the amplitude squared times the phase space of final states available. In other words, gamma is proportional to the magnitude of m^ 2 divided by twice the energy all multiplied by the density of states row. Also, the cross-section sigma is proportional to the magnitude of m^ 2 divided by the flux time row. The flux is the flux of the particle beam. We can use formulas for specific particle configurations assuming M is known. However, how would you find M itself? M is a matrix element that represents the strength and type of fundamental interactions between particles. To find the value of M, physicist Richard Fineman developed rules of scattering. He also developed a system of diagrams creatively named Fineman diagrams that help to represent particle interactions and calculate relevant values for these interactions. These are powerful tools for calculation and they will be discussed later in the series. We now understand why particles decay and how to use physical quantities like decay rate and cross-section to investigate and predict the decays and interactions between different particles in the standard model. These quantities can be tested, for example, with measurements of particle lifetime, allowing physicists to develop a good understanding of standard model particle properties and the types of interactions that occur between them. systems, including the one used by the FBI,   are an extension of the original Henry 
classification. To review, Henry studied   fingerprints extensively and consulted Sir Francis 
Galton in devising a fingerprint classification   system for criminal investigation. Due to Edward 
Henry’s efforts, the first fingerprint bureau in   history was established in Calcutta, India in 
the year 1897. Before learning how fingerprint   classification works, we need to understand two 
basic concepts, ridge counting and ridge tracing.   They are as simple as the names suggest. For 
the former, we count ridges, and for the latter,   we trace ridges. Let’s see how we do it.
In ridge counting, all the ridges between the core   and the delta are counted. We have already learned 
about the core and delta in the tutorial on types   of fingerprint patterns. Recall that the core 
is the central point of a fingerprint pattern,   and the delta is a triangular structure 
present in the pattern as shown here. Now,   the first step of ridge counting involves drawing 
an imaginary line between the core and the delta.   Then, all the ridges that intersect this imaginary 
line are counted. The number of ridges intervening   between the delta and the core is known as the 
ridge count for that pattern. There are also a   few rules we need to remember while counting the 
ridges. First, the exact points of the core and   delta need to be located. This involves a set of 
different rules about what point on the pattern   must be considered the core or the delta. These 
rules are to be followed stringently because   though the ridges on the imaginary line between 
the core and the delta are counted, the core and   the delta are not themselves to be included in 
the ridge count. However, discussing the rules   to establish the core and delta will be beyond 
the scope of this tutorial. When it is said that   all the ridges intervening with the imaginary line 
are to be counted, it does not include incipient   ridges. An incipient ridge is an immature friction 
ridge that will look thinner and shallower than   the ridges surrounding it. They are not considered 
in ridge counting because they may or may not   appear in fingerprint impressions. However, if 
Galton details such as an island or a dot ridge   appear on the imaginary line, they are given one 
ridge count. An abrupt ending of the ridge on the   imaginary line is also given one ridge count. If 
a bifurcation is present on the imaginary line,   the ridge count is two. Even in impressions where 
the point of origin of a bifurcation is present   on the imaginary line, the ridge count is two. 
Similar rules are applied for the rest of the   Galton details present on the imaginary line.
If you recall, a loop pattern has one delta and   one core. So only one imaginary line needs to be 
drawn and subsequently, ridges are counted. But   what about whorls? They have two deltas and 
one core. Therefore, going by this method,   there will be two imaginary lines and two ridge 
counts, one on each side. Which of the two ridge   counts is to be considered in classification? 
Do we take the average of both? Or is the larger   count considered? If there are 10 ridges on one 
side and 12 ridges on the other, is the ridge   count 12 because it is a larger number, or is 
the ridge count 11 because that is the average?   Actually, both of these answers are wrong. This 
is where ridge counting has its limitations and   we move towards ridge tracing for whorl patterns.
Ridge tracing is slightly more complicated than   ridge counting. As the name suggests, a ridge 
is traced. Which ridge? The lower ridge of the   left delta as shown in the pattern here. Here, 
the path of the lower ridge of the left delta   is traced towards the right delta. If the ridge 
ends abruptly, the immediate ridge following the   previous ridge is continued to be traced. 
If the traced ridge ends in a bifurcation,   the lower ridge of the bifurcation is continued 
to be traced. The ridge is traced until it reaches   the point closest to the right delta. Now, 
whorl patterns can be classified depending   on whether the traced ridge falls inside or 
outside of the right delta. Let’s understand   this concept by looking at a few fingerprint 
patterns. In fingerprint pattern A, the course   of the ridge is followed from the left delta 
towards the right delta. This traced course of   the ridge appears to lie inside the right delta. 
Following this, all the ridges intervening between   the traced ridge and the right delta are counted. 
If this ridge count is three or more than three,   the ridge tracing is considered to be “inside” 
and the pattern is described as an “inner whorl”,   denoted with a capital I. As you might observe in 
this particular pattern, there are more than three   ridges between the traced ridge and the right 
delta, which is specifically why pattern A is an   “inner whorl”. Similarly, in pattern B, the traced 
ridge seems to lie outside the right delta. The   ridges intervening between the traced ridge and 
the right delta are counted. If this ridge count   is three or more than three, as is the case with 
this pattern, the ridge tracing is considered to   be “outside” and the pattern is described as an 
“outer whorl”, denoted with a capital O. So what   if less than three ridges are intervening between 
the traced ridge and the right delta? That brings   us to our third classification. If there are 
less than three intervening ridges, it doesn’t   matter whether the traced ridge lies inside or 
outside of the right delta. Such a ridge tracing   is classified as “meeting”, and the pattern as a 
“meet or meeting whorl” denoted with a capital M.  Now that we are familiar with ridge counting 
and tracing, we will learn how to classify   fingerprints based on these concepts. Hopefully 
you have all of your rolled fingerprints ready on   a fingerprint card or a sheet of paper by now. 
Try to perform ridge counting or ridge tracing   on these patterns depending on whether it's a 
loop or a whorl. For a loop, use a pencil for   drawing a line between the core and the delta for 
ridge counting, and then write the resultant ridge   count below it. Similarly, conduct ridge tracing 
on whorl patterns and classify them as inner,   outer, or a meet. But what about arches? 
Just leave them alone for now. And don’t   worry if you’re not able to do it perfectly! What 
matters is whether you’ve understood the procedure   or not. We will use these results for building 
your fingerprint profile in the next tutorial.

**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 6K | **Date:** 1 month ago | **Duration:** 7:09 | **ID:** RJrRH1y2Jz4

In the previous tutorial, we discussed the 
hydroformylation of olefins to produce linear   aldehydes, which are important intermediates 
in the chemical industry. The smallest aldehyde   that can be prepared by hydroformylation is 
propanal, a three carbon synthon. Acetaldehyde,   which contains only two carbon atoms, is 
also an important industrial intermediate,   with a yearly market of 1.4 million tons. Of 
course it can’t be prepared by hydroformylation,   because the product will contain the carbons in 
the olefin as well as the carbon in the carbonyl   that inserts, and there are no olefins with only 
one carbon atom. The main approach to producing   acetaldehyde is called the Wacker reaction. 
The name is derived from the company which   discovered it, which launched in Germany in the 
late 1950s. Wacker was interested in ethylene   as a precursor to functionalized monomers for 
plastic, and they discovered the oxidation of   ethylene in a collaboration with another German 
chemical giant, Hoechst. The plant they opened   in Burghausen in 1978 is still active and has 
produced over 5 million tons of acetaldehyde.  The reaction operates at the gas/liquid interface. 
A gas mixture of ethylene and oxygen is pumped   through an aqueous solution of the catalysts, 
which include sodium tetrachloropalladate   and cupric chloride. The palladium species 
catalyzes the reaction of water with ethylene,   which reduces the Pd(II) to Pd(0), 
and Cu(II) catalyzes the oxygen-driven   reoxidation to Pd(II). The reaction operates 
at fairly high temperature, around 100-130oC,   and moderate pressure of 4-10 atmospheres.
The mechanism has been studied in detail.   The key step is the coordination of Pd(II) with 
ethylene. This scheme represents the mechanism   in a simplified form. The chloropalladate is the 
main form in solution, but the actual catalyst   is species 1, PdCl2. The Pd(II) catalyst first 
coordinates with the olefin to form intermediate   2. The coordination with Pd(II) makes the 
olefin electrophilic, and water can attack   the coordinated olefin as nucleophile to form 
a new C-O bond, yielding 3. This undergoes a   beta-elimination of HPdCl to yield first the enol 
of acetaldehyde, which tautomerizes to give the   more stable carbonyl form. The palladium species 4 
is then converted back to 1 by the elimination of   HCl and reoxidation by CuCl2 and oxygen. More 
precisely, first the Cu(II) converts Pd(0) to   Pd(II) and then oxygen reconverts Cu(I) to Cu(II), 
making the reaction catalytic both in Cu and Pd.  The step leading from 2 to 3 deserves special 
attention, because we have not encountered it   previously. We have mentioned that Pd(II) 
is very electrophilic and coordination with   olefins makes olefins also electrophilic. This is 
unusual, because simple olefins are nucleophilic   and react with electrophiles, like bromine, or 
Bronsted-Lowry acids. Olefin-Pd(II) complexes   are important intermediates in catalysis. Their 
electrophilicity is a consequence of the bonding   pattern, illustrated here. The key interaction 
consists of an electron donation from the filled   olefin pi bond into an empty d orbital, the 
LUMO of Pd(II). There is also some electron back   donation from a filled d orbital of palladium, 
the HOMO, into a pi star olefinic orbital,   but this is not enough to compensate for the 
donation of electron density by the olefin,   which remains electron poor. We can therefore 
generalize the Wacker process, as follows.  The electron poor olefin is attacked by 
a nucleophile from the backside of the   olefin-palladium bond, yielding an intermediate 
which can undergo easy beta-hydride elimination   to yield a substituted olefin. The palladium 
then needs to be reoxidized to re-enter the   cycle. The net effect is replacement of a C-H 
olefinic bond with a carbon-nucleophile bond,   with retention of configuration at the 
olefinic carbon, if the olefin is substituted.   In the classical Wacker case, the nucleophile 
is water. It is reasonable to assume that   other nucleophiles can work as well, thus 
broadening the potential of this chemistry   to other interesting transformations. For 
example, a carboxylate can be the nucleophile,   and this reaction is an important approach 
to vinyl acetate, a valuable monomer for   many commercial polymerization reactions. Alcohols 
can also function as nucleophiles, and under the   acidic conditions used, ketals are usually formed 
from the intermediate vinyl ethers. This example   shows that the Wacker reaction is not limited 
to ethylene but can be extended to most alkenes.  With asymmetrical alkenes, the problem of 
regiochemistry arises. The Wacker reaction   follows Markovnikov selectivity, which means that 
the nucleophile ends up at the carbon which best   stabilizes the incipient positive charge. In 
the first example, the secondary carbenium   ion is more stable than the primary one. In the 
second example the ester function destabilizes an   incipient positive charge at the alpha position 
and the opposite regiochemistry is observed.  As for other examples, using amines as 
nucleophiles is problematic, because they   extensively bind Pd(II) salts and prevent olefin 
coordination with palladium. For this reason,   amine derivatives with reduced basicity are used 
instead, like amides, carbamates, sulfonamides,   and so forth. In the example shown here, 
a lactam, which refers to a cyclic amide,   reacts in excellent yield to produce an enamide. 
Note the use of Cu(I) salts as co-catalysts. They   can also be used, because they are oxidized 
in situ by the oxygen gas to Cu(II). Finally,   the reaction can be used to form cyclic 
systems if the olefin and the nucleophile   are part of the same molecule. Examples of 
cyclo-etherification and cyclo-amination are   shown here. Note the use of sulfonamides as 
protected amines. The corresponding amine in   this case does not work because it is too basic.
There are many more complex examples of Wacker   chemistry in the literature, but these few 
examples should suffice to illustrate the   tremendous potential of olefin-Pd(II) chemistry. 
In conclusion, in addition to its industrial use   for the production of acetaldehyde, Wacker 
chemistry can be extended to a wide array   of synthetic transformations, and it is still 
fertile ground for discovering new chemistry.

## 28. Introduction to Particle Physics: A Tour of the Standard Model
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 34K | **Date:** 1 month ago | **Duration:** 11:54 | **ID:** PUzbjRjOgO4

In this modern physics series, we started out by 
covering the very basics of quantum mechanics,   relativity, and particle physics. Then we returned 
to quantum mechanics with considerably more rigor,   going in-depth with the math and elucidating much 
more of the nuance. Now it’s time to do the same   thing with particle physics. These few initial 
tutorials on QED, QCD, and related topics were   great for getting your feet wet with basic 
terminology and concepts. But now it’s time   to go deeper with particle physics, looking more 
closely at the math and again uncovering more of   the nuance than we were ready to describe before.
The Standard Model of particle physics is arguably   the most successful scientific theory ever 
developed. It predicted the existence and   properties of many particles that were later 
discovered, including the W boson, Z boson, gluon,   top quark, and charm quark. It is also responsible 
for predicting the Higgs mechanism and the Higgs   boson, the most recent major particle discovery. 
On top of all these impressive predictions,   perhaps the Standard Model’s greatest 
accomplishment is its prediction of the   value of the anomalous electron dipole moment. 
This is an intrinsic particle property describing   charge distribution, and it deviates slightly 
from the originally expected value of 2. The   Standard Model predicted this deviation to a 
precision of more than one part per billion,   indicating that the electron is extremely 
well described by this model. However,   humanity didn’t even know about the existence 
of the electron until 1897, when J.J. Thomson   found it using cathode ray tubes like the ones 
found in old TVs. In barely more than 100 years,   how did we go from a model that was developed 
from the first known subatomic particle, to a   complex and intricate theory describing all known 
types of matter and three fundamental forces?  The history of the Standard Model was kickstarted 
by the flurry of particle discoveries in the early   20th century. Ernest Rutherford found protons in 
1911. James Chadwick found neutrons in 1932. Then   Carl Anderson found the first antimatter 
particle, the positron, in the same year.   Within the next two decades, muons and pions 
were found, and particle accelerators started   coming online around the world. With all these new 
discoveries, scientists realized they needed some   way to organize and explain the particles. They 
decided that the best way to do this was to create   a model that could serve as the standard for 
particle physics as the field evolved. Originally,   an arrangement called the Eightfold Way 
was proposed. This took various particles,   largely baryonic, meaning made of quarks, and 
placed them into geometrical patterns. It provided   the first structure for particle physicists to 
follow, and guided the field through the early   1960s. From the success of the Eightfold Way, it 
was eventually discovered that matter was made   up of three types of basic building blocks, 
and with that the Standard Model was born.   It is currently believed that every particle in 
the model is an elementary particle, which means   that it cannot be broken down into smaller parts.
The first group of particles are quarks,   of which there are 6 types: up, down, top, bottom, 
strange, and charm. These quarks make up protons   and neutrons, so they make up most of the mass of 
visible matter in the universe. There are three   generations of quarks. The most stable quarks 
are in the first generation, those are the up   and down quark. These are most of the quarks 
that we see in the universe today. The second   generation contains the strange and charm quark. 
And the third generation contains the bottom and   top quark. Quarks are all charged particles, 
and in the case of the proton and neutron,   the charges of the up and down quarks inside them 
add together to yield the +1 charge of the proton   and the net 0 charge of the neutron. Particles 
involving combinations of three quarks, like the   proton and neutron, are called hadrons. But quarks 
can also be combined in pairs to form mesons.  The next group of particles in the Standard Model 
are leptons. The most well-known lepton is the   electron, which is a first generation lepton. 
The electron has a charge of -1 and is present   in chemical reactions, as it is one of the charged 
constituents of an atom or molecule. The heavier   leptons are the muon and tau particles, which are 
very similar to electrons except for their masses,   and these are second and third generation leptons 
respectively. The final type of lepton remains one   of the more mysterious particles in the Standard 
Model. The neutrino is an extremely light and   neutrally charged lepton, with three flavors: 
the electron neutrino, the muon neutrino, and   the tau neutrino. It was first discovered because 
of a range of energies produced from beta decay,   a process whereby it was believed that a proton 
or neutron emitted a positron or electron. It was   expected that by conservation of energy, these 
electrons and positrons would all be produced   at the same energy, rather than a range. This 
either indicated that energy was not conserved,   or that another particle was being emitted and not 
detected. With an extremely small mass and neutral   charge, neutrinos were proposed as the undetected 
particle to solve the beta decay energy dilemma.   According to the prediction of the Standard 
Model, the neutrino would have no mass. However,   due to the observation of neutrino oscillations 
between different flavors as they propagate   through space, it has been experimentally 
proven that the mass, although very small,   is non-zero. There are also many ongoing 
experiments that are attempting to discover   whether the neutrino is its own antiparticle, 
which would add to its intrigue. Both of these   are examples of physics beyond the Standard Model, 
which we will discuss later. Another thing to   note about the first two groups of particles in 
the Standard Model, the quarks and the leptons,   is that they have half-integer spins. These 
therefore qualify as fermions, since fermions   are particles that can have spins of any half 
integer value like 1/2, 3/2, 5/2, and so forth.  The final group of particles in the Standard Model 
are bosons, which have integer spins of 0, 1, 2,   and so forth. These are the particles that 
mediate interactions between all the others   in the model. This is why bosons are sometimes 
called force carrier particles. The strong force,   which is modeled by quantum chromodynamics, or 
QCD, is mediated by the gluon. This pertains to   interactions between quarks, so the strong force 
occurs on the nuclear scale. Quarks and gluons   both very rarely exist independently and prefer 
to exist bound together inside hadrons or mesons.   The weak force, which is modeled by quantum 
flavordynamics, or QFD, or sometimes together   with electromagnetism as electroweak theory, 
is mediated by the W and Z bosons. As mentioned   previously, the prediction and observation of 
these bosons was a huge victory for the field   of particle physics. One of the best examples 
of a weak force interaction is beta decay.   Finally, the electromagnetic force, which is 
modeled by quantum electrodynamics, or QED,   is mediated by the photon. The photon 
is known widely as the light particle,   and light is composed of oscillating electric 
and magnetic fields that are orthogonal to   one another and propagate through space. As a 
result, any interactions of photons and matter   are governed by QED and electromagnetism.
You may notice that we have one fundamental   force left, and one boson left. However, the 
remaining boson does not mediate the force of   gravity. A quantum theory of gravity has not yet 
been formulated in a way that can be incorporated   into the Standard Model. The best theory of 
gravity that exists today is Einstein’s General   Relativity, which so far has been unable to be 
reconciled with the Standard Model. As a result,   these two extremely well-corroborated 
theories remain separate. We will examine   general relativity in greater depth after 
this investigation of particle physics.  In fact, the final boson is also the most recently 
discovered particle in the Standard Model. The   Higgs was proposed in 1964 by Peter Higgs as 
a field that filled the universe and gave mass   to elementary particles. The Higgs boson would 
be the corresponding particle for this field,   similar to the photon being the corresponding 
particle for an electromagnetic field. The   strength of interaction between a particle 
and this field would dictate how much mass   the particle ended up with, and the particle would 
gain this mass through something called the Higgs   mechanism. This will be discussed in much more 
detail later, but in 2012, the Large Hadron   Collider at CERN was able to produce and observe 
the Higgs boson using data from a large number   of particle collisions. This particle’s discovery 
confirmed that the Higgs field was real and added   a key mass-generating boson to the Standard Model.
Even though the Standard Model has been massively   successful, there are limitations to what 
it can describe. As we mentioned earlier,   gravity doesn’t fit into the model in its current 
state. Additionally, its predictions about the   mass of the neutrino were proven incorrect. 
Other failings of the model include its current   inability to explain dark matter and dark energy. 
As we will see throughout this series, while the   Standard Model isn’t perfect, a truly impressive 
amount of information has been learned about these   subatomic particles as well as how they interact 
with each other and the world around them.   But how do scientists study objects that are 
so small that they can’t be seen even with the   world’s best microscope? The answer is simple. 
Particle accelerators, particle colliders,   and a variety of ingenious detector technologies.
Similar to the Large Hadron Collider at CERN   that smashes hadrons together, which once 
again are made up of three quarks apiece,   there are particle accelerators around the world 
that excite and then direct beams of particles   at each other so that they collide at extremely 
high energies and reveal fascinating physics.   Because the energy scale of colliders reaches far 
beyond what we normally see in the universe today,   these experiments can recreate the conditions of 
the hot and dense early universe, or in some of   the most extreme parts of our universe today. This 
allows for a different angle of studying particles   than just observing the ones present around us at 
this time. However, these conditions only exist   for a tiny fraction of a second, so detectors 
must be phenomenally precise and fine-tuned.   They operate kind of like telescopes, which 
are hit by photons that are manipulated into   a visible image on your eye when you look through 
the eyepiece. These detectors turn energy deposits   or charged paths from a variety of particles 
into electronic signals that can be read out   as the signature of an event. Using a variety of 
computational techniques, the particles and their   trajectories can be reconstructed to show all 
the details of the event that just took place.  Using the powerful theoretical techniques of 
the Standard Model, alongside the sophisticated   experimental techniques employed by particle 
physicists around the world, we’ve learned an   incredible amount about the smallest building 
blocks of our universe. Throughout the process   of learning about these particle constituents 
of our world, scientists have developed new   revolutionary technologies, including computer 
chips, medical imaging and treatment, and the   World Wide Web. As we progress through this 
series, we will learn about all the fascinating   physics that governs Standard Model particles 
and the way that they interact. And we will   also describe how much there still is to discover 
and learn about the field of particle physics.

## 29. Class Sarcopterygii: Lobe-Finned Fishes and Tetrapods
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 8K | **Date:** 1 month ago | **Duration:** 5:26 | **ID:** FuTTBOk50rA
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=FuTTBOk50rA

### Transcript:
Let’s go back to our chordate cladogram. For 
the past several tutorials we’ve been discussing   Actinopterygii, the ray-finned fish. Now let’s 
take a look at its sister clade, Sarcopterygii,   the lobe-finned fish. Extant lobe-finned fish are 
split into three clades: Actinistia, Dipnoi, and   Tetrapoda. Let’s start by going over Actinistia.
There are only two extant members of subclass   Actinistia, and they are both commonly known as 
coelacanths. Coelacanths were once thought to have   gone extinct around 70 million years ago, but in 
1938, a living specimen was caught off the coast   of South Africa. Since then, more individuals 
have been discovered in the Indian Ocean,   off the coasts of South Africa, Madagascar, 
and Comoros. Coelacanths are deep-sea fish that   typically inhabit depths between 100 and 500 
meters. They are known for their distinctive   appearance, which includes four fleshy, limb-like 
fins and a long, tapered tail. They are estimated   to live up to 100 years, based on analysis of 
annual growth marks on scales, and are estimated   to reach sexual maturity around the age of 55.
Subclass Dipnoi contains the lungfish. There are   only six extant species of lungfish, divided 
into three genera: Lepidosiren, Protopterus,   and Neoceratodus. They are found in South America, 
Africa, and Australia. They are primarily known   by their ability to breathe air, presence of 
lobed fins, well-developed internal skeleton,   and ability to aestivate, which essentially means 
to go do dormant for long periods of time and not   dry out, by secreting a mucous cocoon to prevent 
dehydration, and entering a state of suspended   animation with a greatly reduced metabolic rate.
Extant lungfish are the closest living relatives   to the tetrapods and their fossil history extends 
back some 410 million years. Living forms all have   an elongated body with fleshy, paired pectoral 
and pelvic fins and a single unpaired caudal   fin. Their unique respiratory system includes 
lungs that are subdivided into numerous air sacs,   and most species have two lungs, except for 
the Australian which has only one. Of the   extant lungfish, only the Australian lungfish can 
breathe through its gills without needing air from   its lungs. In other species, the gills are too 
atrophied to allow for adequate gas exchange.   Thus, as adults, five of the six extant species 
of lungfish must breathe air. This means they   can drown, just like us, and as such, they are a 
fascinating link in the evolutionary history of   the last group of lobe-finned fish, the tetrapods.
Finally, Tetrapoda includes a great deal of   extinct species, as well as all modern amphibians, 
reptiles, birds, and mammals, meaning all extant   tetrapods are more closely related to each other 
than any non-tetrapods. This means that snakes   are more closely related to humans than they 
are to eels, even though they look kind of   similar to eels, and whales are more closely 
related to frogs than they are sharks, even   though whales superficially resemble fish. That 
is because all tetrapods share common ancestry,   with the last common ancestor of all tetrapods 
dating back to about 400 million years ago.  There are many fossil forms that illustrate 
the evolution from obligate water dwelling   species into terrestrial forms, but at least one 
extinct species of great importance is Tiktaalik,   an extinct lobe-finned fish from the 
late Devonian. Though technically a fish,   it had a large flattened head with eyes 
on top, instead of along the sides,   and fins that were closer morphologically to 
tetrapod limbs. It is an important transitional   fossil in the evolution of vertebrates from water 
to land which has provided important insights into   the evolutionary history of vertebrates, and 
has helped scientists better understand how   fish gradually adapted to life on land.
It’s important to remember that ancient   lobe-finned fish were not the first organisms 
to colonize the land. Bacteria, fungi, plants,   and even other animals, like the arthropods and 
gastropods, had already been living on land for   millions of years before Tiktaalik. Also, 
Tiktaalik and its kin didn’t just flop onto   land. They still needed the water to survive, 
so they couldn’t migrate too far away. In fact,   complete domination of the land by the vertebrates 
wouldn’t happen for millions of years with the   evolution of the amniotes. But we aren’t quite 
there yet. For now, that wraps up a summary of the   lobe-finned fishes. Remember that cladistically, 
all tetrapods are also lobe finned fishes,   but that description doesn’t really help 
much. In the next tutorial, we will begin   to examine the only extant clade of tetrapods 
that aren’t also amniotes, the amphibians,   who spread further into the terrestrial 
environment than the ancient sarcopterygians.

So far in this series on world history, we have 
been looking exclusively at the European, Asian,   and African continents. But what was happening 
over in the western hemisphere during this time?   The Olmecs, who are now often described 
as the first Mesoamerican civilization,   were a people who occupied the coastal area of the 
Gulf of Mexico from around the 6th millennium BCE;   but it was between 1600 and 400 BCE that they 
developed an organized society based on cities   and institutions that would go on to influence 
their rough contemporaries, the Maya, as well   as much later civilizations like the Aztec Empire 
of the 15th and 16th centuries CE. Because we have   relatively little archeological evidence from the 
Olmec civilization itself, and no written records   of the sort associated with the Maya, there is 
some debate over how many of the institutions   known from those later civilizations were 
already a part of Olmec life. In fact, “Olmec”,   which means “rubber people”, was not their 
name for themselves, but was taken by scholars   from the Aztec name for the people who lived in 
the same coastal region during their own time.  The Olmecs inhabited a few large cities near the 
coast as well as villages located upland along   the Coatzacoalcos river. Until the 10th century 
BCE, the primary Olmec city was in the location   now occupied by San Lorenzo in the Mexican state 
of Veracruz. This was then abandoned, possibly   due to farmland becoming infertile, and a new city 
was created at the site of La Venta in the state   of Tabasco. This city featured a pyramid which 
was the largest structure of ancient Mesoamerica.   There were also two other Olmec sites in the same 
region, at Tres Zapotes and Laguna de los Cerros.   Olmec cities, however, were not large population 
centers but places of worship. San Lorenzo had   only a couple hundred dwellings, while everyone 
else lived in smaller villages farther upland,   and there is no evidence that these cities 
controlled or dominated nearby settlements   as cities in Mesopotamia and Egypt did. The most 
famous features of Olmec cities are the colossal   stone heads that were set up there, which weigh 
between 30 and 60 tons each. Because each of   these heads has its own individual features, 
they are thought to represent specific people,   presumably leaders of the community; but they also 
wear helmets, which suggests that they were being   depicted as players of the ball game that was 
popular across ancient Mesoamerica. The balls   used in this game were made of rubber, which was 
produced from the latex taken from trees in Olmec   territory; and though no ballcourts or pictorial 
representations of the game have been found   in Olmec territory, rubber balls from that time 
have been recovered from the Coatzacoalcos river.  In addition to stone heads, Olmec craftsmen 
produced free-standing sculptures of human   figures, and stone slabs that depicted people 
in various scenes. Many of their sculpted works   were naturalistic in appearance, though they might 
also incorporate the facial features of jaguars,   which were an important part of Olmec religion. 
They also made painted and incised pottery, as   well as luxury objects like masks, figurines, iron 
mirrors, axes, and knives, which were symbolic   objects rather than actual weapons. These objects 
were made out of precious materials like jade and   obsidian, and they are evidence of an extensive 
Olmec trading network which spread across Mexico   and into Guatemala. The materials used to make 
them were, in turn, brought to Olmec territory   from sources hundreds of miles away. A number of 
sites which may have been Olmec settlements have   been found along these Mexican trading routes.
The Olmecs produced several cultural innovations   that were then adopted by other civilizations in 
the region. One of these was a calendar with a   365-day solar count, as well as a 260-day count 
that may have been used for religious festivals.   This had 20 periods of 13 days, each of which 
was dedicated to a specific deity. The 365-day   calendar was used for agriculture because it 
aligned with the seasons. It consisted of 18   periods of 20 days, each with its own name, plus 
five unnamed days at the end of the year. This   system was later used by both the Maya and Aztec 
civilizations. The Olmec may also have used a form   of the “Long Count” system used to record dates 
of up to hundreds of years on Mayan monuments.   This count was based on the number of days since 
the creation of the world, represented in units   from a single day to groups of 20, and then to 
groups of these groups, generally ending with the   b’akt’un which equaled 144,000 days or about 394 
years. To represent a specific date, it recorded   the appropriate number of each of these groups 
of days in columns from largest to smallest,   using the equivalent of a zero for empty columns. 
Though we do not have any monuments that use this   system from the time of the Olmecs themselves, 
several of the earliest examples of it do come   from what had once been Olmec territory.

of pictorial symbols, one with 62 characters, have   recently been discovered in Olmec territory; but 
there is nothing comparable that might be used to   interpret them. We are not certain about what kind 
of language the Olmecs spoke, though many scholars   now believe it was a member of the Mixe-Zoquean 
family of languages, because these are now spoken   in what was Olmec territory; and Mixe-Zoquean 
words are found in other Mesoamerican languages,   which suggests that they entered them along 
with other aspects of Olmec art and culture.  One of the more controversial questions asked 
about Olmec society is whether it practiced   the sort of human sacrifice that was common in 
some other Mesoamerican civilizations. There is   some evidence that the Olmecs practiced 
bloodletting, because the sort of sharp   spikes used elsewhere for this purpose

moves from one center to another, may have had to   do with changes in the local rivers which meant

the culture itself came to an end, only that   it continued on in smaller communities. At the

separate valleys and were often at war with one   another. Then, around the year 600, a new city was 
built on the site of Monte Alban which overlooked   all three valleys. This became an urban center 
for the entire region, and beginning around 400   BCE the Zapotecs began to expand beyond their own 
borders and to conquer the surrounding regions.   Their style of pottery quickly replaced 
the styles of the areas they controlled,   which suggests they were colonizing them; and 
for centuries Monte Alban was the largest and   most powerful city in the region. A series of 
reliefs carved in a building in the city center   seems to represent the former chiefs of all 
of these new Zapotec territories, and implies   that those who resisted were sacrificed, 
while those who cooperated were spared.   This empire persisted until the arrival 
of Spanish forces in the 16th century CE,   and even then the locals continued to resist their 
rule. Among the Zapotec innovations was a system   of writing that was entirely different from that 
of the Olmecs. Though it has not been deciphered,   it appears to be the source of the later scripts 
used by the Mayans and Aztecs, and like those   was a syllabic system in which each symbol 
represented a syllable of the Zapotec language.  Beginning around 100 CE, a culture now described 
as Classic Veracruz developed slightly to the   north of the Olmec heartland. The remains of 
this culture show some traces of Olmec influence,   in particular the ball game. A number of 
stone ballcourts have been found in this area,   which were decorated with reliefs depicting the 
players and their equipment. Like the Olmecs,   the Veracruz culture had cities that were 
ritual sites but not residential centers,   and they produced both stone monuments and 
luxury objects which they traded over great   distances. They also had a developed ceramic 
culture, and made pottery painted with scenes,   as well as elaborately decorated figurines. 
Like the Olmecs, they practiced bloodletting,   but unlike them they left explicit evidence 
that they also engaged in human sacrifice.  During the same centuries that the Olmec and then 
the Zapotec societies developed and flourished,   a network of cities, which was centered on the 
Yucatan to the east, was beginning to appear.   This was the first growth of Maya society, 
which in the centuries that followed would   become the first large-scale civilization to

## 35. Diversity of the Ray-Finned Fishes Part 3: Percomorpha and Perciformes
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 5K | **Date:** 2 months ago | **Duration:** 11:57 | **ID:** CUmcpz7BtaA
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=CUmcpz7BtaA

### Transcript:
For several tutorials we have been examining the 
diversity of the ray-finned fishes, and we have   gone through many of the important clades, only 
to arrive at Percomorpha. Members of Percomorpha   are often referred to as the “perch shaped” 
or “perch-like” fish, and this is where they   get their name. The clade is not only extremely 
diverse, but also recently evolved. As a clade,   they diverged from all other ray-finned a 
little less than 100 million years ago, and they   continued to diversify both before and immediately 
after the mass extinction event that paved the way   for the Cenozoic. They likely found themselves 
survivors in a dramatically altered ocean,   and quickly diversified to fill many niches. 
The evolutionary relationships between their   orders are complex, and some relationships are 
still debated, though it is widely accepted that   Percomorpha is a monophyletic clade. Previously, 
this entire clade was considered a single order   called Perciformes, while some of the orders 
that follow are still considered to be unranked,   and their order names disputed. We will 
discuss all potential orders to make this   as exhaustive as possible, so let’s get started.
Members of order Ophidiiformes have small heads   and long slender bodies. They have either smooth 
scales or no scales, a long dorsal fin, and an   anal fin that typically runs into the caudal 
fin. They include the cusk-eels, pearlfishes,   and brotulas. The Batrachoidiformes include a 
single family of toadfish, or frogfish, which are   benthic ambush predators, the males of which are 
capable of “singing” by using their swim bladder   as a sound-production device. Order Kurtiformes 
includes the nurseryfishes and cardinalfishes,   which are distinguished by their large mouths, and 
the division of the dorsal fin into two separate   fins. Gobiiformes are closely related and includes 
the gobies and their relatives, most of which are   small species that live in marine water and are 
primarily benthic or burrowing fishes. Meanwhile,   order Scombriformes includes much larger species, 
such as the tuna and mackerel. Many species are   noted for their streamlined bodies, abilities to 
reach high speeds, high intelligence, and apparent   endothermy, meaning tuna can keep their internal 
temperature higher than the surrounding waters.  Members of the closely related order 
Syngnathiformes includes many familiar   and charismatic species such as the seahorses, 
pipefishes, and seadragons. They are characterized   by their elongated bodies, tubular snouts, and 
unique courtship and reproductive behaviors.   Many species have prolonged courtship rituals that 
include elaborate dances, synchronized movements,   daily greetings, and of course, in some 
species, after mating, the female passes   the eggs into the male’s brood pouch where they 
hatch, and the male gives birth to the young.  Moving on, Synbranchiformes includes the swamp 
eels, and Anabantiformes includes the snakeheads,   Siamese fighting fish, and gouramies, which 
are charactered by their labyrinth organ,   a specialized structure that allows them 
to breathe air directly from the surface,   meaning they can survive in areas of 
stagnant water and low oxygen. Some,   like the Siamese fighting fish, are popular 
aquarium fish that require a great deal more care   than is often advertised. Carangiformes includes 
the jacks, pompanos, jack mackerels, runners,   trevallies, and scads. The Pleuronectiformes 
are also known as flatfish, which as adults,   have both eyes located on one side of the head, 
allowing them to lie flat on the ocean floor,   making them asymmetrical vertebrates, though 
they are bilaterally symmetrical as larvae,   and undergo metamorphosis to become asymmetrical. 
In contrast to these asymmetrical adults,   the mullets of order Mugiliformes are symmetrical, 
silvery, have two separate dorsal fins, triangular   mouths, and are found in oceans worldwide.
Next up, order Cichliformes includes the   convict blennies and the highly diverse cichlids. 
Beloniformes includes the ricefish, needlefish,   flyingfishes, and halfbeaks. Some of the most 
famous members of this clade, the flying fish,   can make powerful, self-propelled leaps 
out of the water where their long wing-like   fins enable gliding for considerable 
distances above the water's surface.  Members of order Atheriniformes are often known 
as silversides, while the Cyprinodontiformes are   mainly small, freshwater fish that include 
a number of popular aquarium fish like the   killifish, and other live-bearers such as 
the guppy, that give birth to live young   after holding the eggs within their bodies. The 
Lophiiformes are often simply known as anglerfish,   which are characterized by their large mouths 
and expandable stomachs. They exhibit extreme   sexual dimorphism where females are large and 
distinct while the males are much smaller and   permanently attached to the females, acting as 
a parasitic mate. They also have a unique and   highly specialized feeding apparatus, as well 
as a modified dorsal fin ray that extends above   their mouths and functions as a lure to attract 
prey. Their typical habitat is the deep sea.  Order Tetraodontiformes include the pufferfish, 
which is characterized by its ability to inflate   its body into a ball-like shape as a defense 
mechanism, along with the triggerfishes,   which have a distinct body shape and are known 
for their sharp teeth and powerful jaws, allowing   them to feed on a variety of prey, including 
crustaceans and hard-shelled invertebrates.   The Scorpaeniformes are known as the “mail-cheeked 
fishes” and include the lionfishes and sculpins,   all of which are carnivorous and often live on 
the sea bottom in relatively shallow waters.   Two prominent groups within this order are the 
scorpionfishes, which are characterized by their   venomous spines and elaborate camouflage patterns 
that help them blend into their surroundings,   and the sea robins which are characterized 
by their specialized pectoral fins that   allow them to "walk" along the seafloor.
Istiophoriformes includes the barracudas,   swordfish, spearfish, marlins, and sailfish, many 
of which are highly migratory, and pelagic species   found in tropical and subtropical waters, 
characterized by their long, slender bodies   and elongated bills or rostrums, often noted for 
their predatory nature and impressive speed and   agility. Order Moroniformes includes the temperate 
basses, sicklefishes, and spadefishes of family   Ephippidae, though the spadefish are sometimes 
treated as a separate order or unplaced family.  Order Trachiniformes includes the swallowers, 
gapers, sandperch, duckbills, stargazers,   and weeverfishes, though its classification 
may be polyphyletic and studies have suggested   breaking different members into the orders 
Scombriformes, with the tuna and mackerel,   Gobiiformes, or the gobies, and also 
forming two new orders: Uranoscopiformes,   and Pempheriformes. Controversies like this abound 
in Percomorpha. For example, order Spariformes   is often cited as including the breams, porgies, 
and tripletails, but the tripletails may actually   belong to their own order, Lobotiformes.
There are also a number of smaller orders   within Percomorpha, some of which may have 
uncertain placements, while others have long   been confirmed to be monphyletic. These are the 
Gobiesociformes which includes the clingfishes,   Blenniiformes or the blennies, Icosteiformes or 
the ragfishes, Callionymiformes or the dragonets,   Scombrolabraciformes which contains a single 
species of longfin escolar or black mackerel,   Caproiformes or the boarfishes, and Labriformes 
or the wrasses, cales, and parrotfish.  Finally, order Perciformes is still 
sometimes used as a synonym for Percomorpha,   and if considered as such, then all of the orders 
in this tutorial fall under Perciformes. However,   this is likely a paraphyletic classification, 
and more evidence has placed Perciformes as   an order within Percomorpha. As it stands, the 
most common and well-known members of this order   are the perch, darters, sea bass, and groupers. 
Sometimes members of Scorpaeniformes, the scorpion   fish, Tetraodontiformes, the pufferfish and 
triggerfish, and Pleuronectiformes, the flatfish,   are listed as suborders of Perciformes rather than 
their own orders. As a whole, order Perciformes,   even if placed as an order within Percomorpha, 
still includes a great deal of diversity.   Consider the archerfish, which are known for 
their unique predation technique of "shooting   down" land-based insects and other small prey 
with jets of water that they spit from their   specialized mouths. Then there are the sweepers, 
the snappers, the snooks, sea chubs, moonfishes,   angelfish, grunts, trumpeters, rabbitfish, 
threadfins and many others. In addition,   there are some groups which are sometimes listed 
as part of Perciformes and sometimes as their own   order. The majorras are sometimes placed as a 
family within Perciformes, and other times as   their own order Gerreiformes. The sunfish are 
sometimes listed as order Centrarchiformes,   and the bigeyes are sometimes considered to be 
an order of their own called Priacanthiformes.  There are also several families within 
Percomorpha, but outside of Perciformes   with uncertain placements, meaning there is not 
yet widespread consensus as to which order they   may fit under, or if they deserve an order 
of their own. This includes Ambassidae,   the glassfish or “perchlets,” Pseudochromidae or 
dottybacks, the damselfishes and anemone fish of   Pomacentridae, the basslets of Grammatidae, 
and the jawfishes of Opistognathidae,   along with many others, such as Acanthuriformes, 
which is sometimes treated as their own order and   split into unplaced families and existing orders.
Now, it’s very important to keep in mind the   magnitude of these revisions. This is not 
occurring at the species or genus level,   this is revision at the order level. Animals of 
the same class but different order are generally   quite different from each other. Think of the 
butterflies of order Lepidoptera and compare   them to the beetles of coleoptera. They’re both 
insects, but they’re quite different. Or imagine   us, humans of the order Primates compared to the 
manatees of order Sirenia. We’re both mammals,   but clearly very different. This isn’t to 
say that physical differences necessarily   indicate different orders, but it’s very 
important to remember that the ray-finned   fish are incredibly diverse. Though many of us 
may just know them as “fish”, the differences   between and within clades is often astounding 
and sometimes entirely overlooked. And with that,   we wrap up the diversity of the ray-finned 
fishes. That means it’s time to move forward   and examine class Sarcopterygii, their sister 
clade, which includes the lobe-finned fishes   and their tetrapod descendants. Let’s 
move forward and check out this clade now.
