Continuing with our study of fingerprints 
as a method of identification, after the   fingerprints are formed at the CS, they get 
subjected to different environmental factors   until the investigating team arrives at the 
scene. This process is called the aging of   the fingerprints. Many of the prints may get 
destroyed and contaminated during this period.   The investigating team must recognize all probable 
sites where fingerprints might be deposited. This   initial examination can be done using alternate 
light sources. Some of the fingerprints might be   readily visible at this stage. Regardless, initial 
examination of the fingerprints is followed by   their enhancement using different techniques. 
Enhancement results in sufficient contrast   between a fingerprint and its surface such that 
all ridge details are readily visible. A complete   fingerprint with a discernable core and delta is 
rarely present at a crime scene. Most of the time,   the fingermarks at the scene are just a small part 
of the fingerprint which may not even establish   the particular pattern. Individualization at 
this stage is out of the question. However,   the investigating team needs to make the most 
of whatever is present at the scene. Therefore,   enhancement of the fingerprints is extremely 
necessary to identify as many Galton details   as possible. After enhancement and subsequent 
recording, these fingerprints are compared   with those of the people suspected to be 
involved in the crime. The enhancement of   fingerprints is a vast topic, and it involves 
many techniques used on different surfaces. We   will study them in detail later in the series. 
For now, the collection of fingerprints from   the suspects is an equally important topic to 
discuss. If proper protocol is not followed,   the fingerprints recorded might be smudged, 
rendering the ridge details incomprehensible.   What if fingermarks collected from the 
scene contain ridge details that match   with the part of the recorded fingerprint that got 
smudged? Recording fingerprints is a non-invasive   procedure, so it does not warrant any harm to the 
subject, nor does it involve the introduction of   any tool inside your body as with collection of 
blood. But attempting to collect fingerprints   from the same subject, again and again, would 
certainly annoy the subject, leading them to   not want to cooperate with the investigation. 
This makes the case for accurate recording of   fingerprints even stronger. Therefore, let 
us learn about this procedure in detail.  Legible fingerprints can be recorded manually 
or digitally. Let’s start with the manual method   first. You can try this at home if you have a 
stamp pad. Use it to take multiple fingerprints   of the same finger on a plain sheet of paper. 
You will observe that the fingerprints taken   later will be more legible due to the evenness 
of the ink deposit. Take a magnifying glass,   or capture a photo of the fingerprint. Zoom 
in to observe the ridge details. Does this   fingerprint contain all the details necessary for 
comparison? Consider this. Hold a pen or pencil   and mimic your action of writing. Use your index 
and middle fingers to mimic smoking. Touch the   screen of your smartphone. Now, consider the pen 
and your smartphone as evidence found at the CS.   What kinds of fingerprints would be detected 
on them? The side of your index finger comes   in contact with a pen while writing. Sides of the 
index and middle finger while smoking. The tip of   the finger is often used to touch the screen. The 
ridge details along with the side parts of the   fingertips, and from the tip of the fingers 
would be recovered from this evidence. Now,   back to your plain fingerprint taken using the 
stamp pad. Can you compare this fingerprint with   the side fingermarks recovered from the pen which 
you just considered as evidence? No, because plain   prints just depict the front-facing part of a 
fingerprint. This is the biggest drawback of using   plain fingerprints for comparison. Sometimes, 
plain fingerprints might not even record a   delta. Counting ridges between the core and the 
delta, and tracing a ridge between two deltas, are   essential aspects of fingerprint classification. 
Coming back to plain prints, they might be the   easiest to collect and the most recovered 
type of fingerprints from a CS. Nevertheless,   a plain print cannot suffice for subsequent 
classification. This is why we need to record a   legible fingerprint that contains all the details 
required for classification. It is fingerprint   classification that will provide a unique identity 
to a person. Therefore, to make things easier by   recording as many ridge details as possible, 
we record fingerprints not only by taking plain   prints but also by rolling the finger from nail 
to nail. These prints are known as rolled prints.   Let us understand how these prints are taken.
First let’s understand that fingerprints are   not recorded by the subject themselves. The 
subject barely has to do anything other than   just cooperate with the procedure. It is the 
investigator who does all the work. The protocol   begins with cleaning the subject’s fingers with 
soap and water so that the fingers are devoid of   grease and contaminants. If soap is unavailable, 
rubbing alcohol can also be used for cleaning.   Some people can have dry and flaky palms. In 
such a case, a hand lotion can be used to wipe   off dust or skin flakes. Once the hands are clean, 
recording begins. An ink pad is placed on a firm   platform in such a way that the forearm should 
be parallel to the ground. In case an ink pad is   not available, a roller is used to roll ink on a 
glass slab. The ink is evenly spread on the glass   slab using the roller. This slab is then used in 
place of an ink pad. The investigator then holds   the finger of the subject and rolls it from nail 
to nail on the ink pad. The fingers are rolled in   such a way that the portion of the finger from 
one edge of the nail to the other, and the area   between the tip of the finger to the crease of 
the first joint, is evenly covered with ink.   The uniformity of ink is very important here as 
otherwise, the pattern will appear smudged. Once   the finger is sufficiently inked, it is rolled on 
the fingerprint card to record the impression. To   prevent smudging, rolling of the finger must be 
done in a continuous motion and the finger must   be lifted immediately after rolling. Another 
important aspect to consider is the sufficient   pressure essential for capturing a legible 
fingerprint. The weight of the fingers alone   is the maximum pressure required for taking clear 
fingerprints. If even a little extra pressure is   applied by the investigator or the subject on 
the fingers, then the fingerprints might not be   accurately recorded. Because of this, the fingers 
are always rolled from an awkward to easy position   to take maximum advantage of the natural movement 
of the forearm. Therefore, the thumb is rolled   towards the center of the body, while the rest 
of the fingers are rolled away from the center   of the body. Just try doing this yourself. Place 
your thumb on a platform and roll it towards the   body as well as away from the body. You will feel 
the transition from a difficult position to an   easier position when you roll the thumb towards 
the body. Try taking rolled fingerprints in both   of these cases, and decide for yourself 
which print looks better. Moving forward,   the investigator must also instruct the subject 
to be loose, not to look at the ink pad, and   focus on something else. The subject might just 
be asked to keep focusing on a spot on the wall   during the entire process. This is because if the 
subject pays attention to actual fingerprinting,   they might become conscious of the procedure, 
leading to extra pressure on the finger. Even   a tiny bit of extra pressure or movement 
might result in insufficient ridge details.  Now that we’ve studied how to record rolled 
fingerprints, let us look at the standard   fingerprint card which is used for recording. The 
first portion involves details of the subject,   including name, residence, alias, the reason 
for fingerprinting, and so on. Below the   details section are two rows. The upper row 
is for fingers of the right hand, numbered 1   to 5 from right thumb to right little finger. 
The lower row is for fingers of the left hand,   numbered 6 to 10 from left thumb to left little 
finger. This section is for rolled fingerprints   and the fingers are rolled in their respective 
blocks. Also, they must be upright and vertical.   Below the rolled prints is the part where plain 
prints are taken. They are taken after the rolled   prints. Four fingers of a hand are pressed 
simultaneously in the section allotted for   the left and right hand. This is followed by the 
recording of the plain prints of the individual   thumbs. One might wonder, what is the need for 
plain prints when we’ve already recorded rolled   prints in detail? Moreover, why not record 
the prints of the four fingers individually,   rather than simultaneously doing the same? The 
reason why these prints are taken simultaneously   is that it helps to verify the sequence of the 
rolled prints with plain prints. In simple words,   rolled fingerprints are compared with the 
corresponding plain print to confirm they’re   from the same finger. Once all fingerprints 
are successfully recorded, they are digitally   scanned to a database. With the manual recording 
of fingerprints done, let’s move on to the digital   method. The protocol of capturing the fingerprints 
is the same here, the only difference being that   the Livescan machine gives real-time feedback 
regarding the clarity of the fingerprints. Thus,   digital recording is a much easier process.
Now, there are some special circumstances that   an investigator might encounter while recording 
fingerprints. If a finger is deformed, every   attempt is made to record rolled and plain prints. 
A tool used in postmortem fingerprinting, known   as the spoon is used for this purpose. If it is 
still impossible to record a legible fingerprint,   the reason is noted in the respective block. 
Similarly, if a finger is missing, it is noted   as such, whether bandaged, paralyzed, injured, 
crippled, et cetera. One thing to mention here is   that the term missing finger does not mean that 
a finger is missing. It just indicates that the   finger is not available for fingerprinting due to 
the presence of a condition that renders it unable   to do so. An amputated finger is noted separately 
along with the reason as amputated, missing since   birth, severed, et cetera. Scarred fingers are 
recorded without any notation. If an individual   has an extra finger, only the thumb and the next 
four fingers are recorded. The extra fingerprint   is not recorded in any case. Some individuals may 
have thin and worn ridges in the pattern area,   due to the nature of their occupation or their 
age. In such a case the ridges are raised by a   technique known as milking the finger. It involves 
rubbing the fingers in a downward motion from palm   to fingertip. If you want to try this process on 
your own, it’s quite easy to download an official   fingerprint card, or you can draw the blocks for 
rolled prints and plain prints on a blank sheet   of paper. Take your fingerprints in the manner 
explained here, or those of someone else. Don’t   worry if they’re not clear enough, we’re just 
attempting to learn the science while having   some fun. After recording, keep the card safe for 
the next tutorial, where we will learn about ridge   counting and ridge tracing, the two most important 
prerequisites for fingerprint classification.

## 39. Ancient China Part 3: The Qin and Han Dynasties (200 BCE – 200 CE)
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 8K | **Date:** 2 months ago | **Duration:** 15:50 | **ID:** FaSceDlR7e4

The Qin state, which was one of the “seven warring 
states” of 5th and 4th centuries BCE China,   developed a powerful centralized government and 
gathered a large force of farmers and soldiers;   and in the second half of the 3rd century BCE, 
it defeated the other six states one by one. In   the year 221 BCE, the Qin king Zheng conquered 
the small territory which was all that was left   of the Zhou kingdom that had ruled all seven 
states, and he renamed himself Shih Huangdi,   the first emperor. He went on to expand 
his domains as far south as Vietnam,   though he was less successful at conquering the 
nomadic horsemen who lived to the north. Thousands   of defeated captives were resettled as colonists 
on his new territories, and the weapons of all   enemy soldiers were confiscated and melted down.
One of the important innovations of the Qin period   was the standardization across the empire, 
of the size and shape of Chinese characters,   which was carried out by the Qin chancellor 
Li Si. He also invented a style of calligraphy   that became very widespread. The creation of 
empire-wide standards in writing, weights and   measures, and the generally centralized character 
of Qin government, reflected the fact that it was   heavily influenced by the philosophical school of 
Legalism, which had developed during the Warring   States period. It also tended to rule the empire’s 
inhabitants with a heavy hand, and to severely   punish them if they disobeyed the authorities. 
The first emperor divided his realm into districts   that were governed by qualified administrators 
rather than members of the royal family,   as had been the case in the Zhou period; and the 
imperial court exercised direct control over the   empire, which was a marked departure from the 
decentralized fengjian system of the Zhou period.   This emphasis on centralization, and on choosing 
administrators by merit rather than by pedigree,   was adopted by subsequent dynasties which 
admired the Qin even though it was autocratic   and rejected Confucianism in favor of Legalism.
The Qin military took even further the innovations   in iron weaponry, cavalry tactics, and the 
use of crossbows that had developed during   the Warring States period. But most famously, the 
first emperor built fortifications to protect the   northern border against the barbarians he had 
been unable to defeat. These became the basis   of the Great Wall, which in its current form 
was built in the 14th and 15th centuries CE.   He also created a defense force to protect 
him after his death, the terracotta army   buried with him in his tomb near the capital 
of Xianyang, which was discovered in 1974.  The Qin dynasty’s embrace of Legalism also 
meant that other philosophical schools,   such as Confucianism and Mohism, were actively 
suppressed. In fact, the narrative called The   Records of the Grand Historian, which was written 
during the Han period, claims that the first Qin   emperor ordered the destruction of books that 
expressed philosophies other than Legalism,   unless they dealt with practical subjects like 
medicine; and had the scholars who resisted this   directive put to death. But because this policy is 
not mentioned in any of our contemporary sources,   it is now thought to have been a later invention.
Though the Qin dynasty was an important influence   on the Han and the others that followed it, it 
was extremely brief. Shih Huangdi died in 210 BCE,   and his advisers tried to replace him with one 
of his sons, whom they were able to manipulate;   but this son, and another member of the 
emperor’s family who quickly succeeded him,   angered the nobility by raising taxes, 
spending money lavishly, and executing   many local officials. A series of rebellions broke 
out, and by 207, the Qin dynasty had been replaced   by the rebel leaders Xiang Yu and Liu Bang, who 
were from the states of Chu and Han respectively.   These two men fought each other while attempting 
to conquer the other remaining states, and in 202   Liu Bang defeated his rival and declared himself 
the first Han emperor under the name Gaozu.  Before this happened, Xiang Yu decided to reverse 
the Qin policy of centralization by dividing his   territories into 18 fengjian states which were 
mostly autonomous, though there was also territory   that was directly controlled by the emperor. He 
put a group of generals, nobles, and members of   his family in charge of the 18 states. While the 
first two were referred to as the yixing wang,   or “kings of different family names”, the third 
was known as tongxing wang, “kings of the same   family name”. When Liu Bang became emperor, he 
did the same thing with his own family and allies,   but he came to regret this decision, and over the 
next fifty years the power of the yixing wang was   slowly diminished. The tongxing wang, on the other 
hand, were left alone until the middle of the 2nd   century BCE, when the emperor Jing decided 
to punish several of his powerful relatives   by reducing the territory of the states they 
ruled. These relatives, who had their own armies,   responded by staging an uprising called the 
“Rebellion of the Seven States” in 154 BCE,   after which Jing restricted their power 
and reduced the size of their domains.  During the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, the Han 
empire was faced with frequent attacks from the   north by an alliance of nomadic tribes they 
called the Xiongnu, who lived in the region   of Mongolia. After an invasion in 200 BCE, the 
two sides signed a treaty as equal partners;   but in practice China was forced to pay the 
tribes large amounts of goods, and even then   some of them continued to launch raids south of 
the border. Toward the end of the 2nd century,   Chinese forces began to defeat the Xiongnu, 
and managed to force them to retreat. They also   incorporated their territory in central Asia, and 
settled it with colonists. At the same time, the   empire was extended southward into southern China, 
and the northern parts of Korea and Vietnam.  During the later 3rd century, a diplomat named 
Zhang Qian visited several states in Central Asia   and northern India, and Han ambassadors 
were eventually sent to these places.   The trade relationships that developed from these 
interactions were the beginnings of the Silk Road,   which eventually ran through Central Asia to 
the Parthian Empire and the Mediterranean coast,   and opened up trade between China and 
the Roman Empire. The Hans also began a   military alliance with the Kushan Empire 
in northern India, and exchanged gifts   with the rulers of Parthia, Burma, and Japan.
In the 1st century BCE there was a change in   government policy. Whereas the “Modernist” faction 
that had dominated during Emperor Wu’s reign in   the late 2nd and early 1st centuries favored the 
conquest of new territories, which was paid for by   government monopolies over commodities like salt 
and iron, by the mid-1st century they had lost   ground to the Reformists, who supported lowering 
taxes and maintaining the current borders.   Emperor Wu also instigated a change in the court’s 
philosophical underpinnings, which until his time   had been a combination of Confucianism and 
Legalism. He declared that only Confucian   scholarship should be recognized, and established 
an Imperial University to train new bureaucrats in   its principles. It was at this time that the 
Records of the Grand Historian was written,   as well as a number of Chinese dictionaries.
There was a brief break in the Han dynasty   between 9 and 23 CE, when a court official 
named Wang Mang, who had been appointed as   the temporary head of government until the new 
emperor, who was a child, could come of age,   declared that he now had the mandate of Heaven and 
was founding his own dynasty, called Xin. He began   by reforming government policy. He redistributed 
land to the peasants and banned slavery,   changes that alienated the aristocracy. He 
was then faced with an uprising of bandits   who had been farmers but were forced off their 
land by massive floods along the Yellow River,   which overwhelmed the dams that had been built to 
contain it. Wang Mang was killed in a riot in 23,   and after two years a member of the Han family 
was able to defeat the bandits and restore the Han   dynasty as Emperor Guangwu. He also recovered the 
territories in Korea and Vietnam that had taken   advantage of the change in government to reassert 
their independence, and attacked the Xiongnu who   had abandoned their arrangements with the Han. 
Because he moved the capital eastward from Xian   to Luoyang, the two halves of the Han dynasty 
are often referred to as western and eastern.  The effectiveness of the imperial court was 
hampered in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE by a   series of plots and intrigues involving the 
dowager empresses, the emperor’s consorts,   and the powerful court eunuchs. The dowager was 
the mother or the widow of a deceased emperor,   and if the emperor’s heir should assume 
the throne when he was still a child,   then she or one of her male relatives might 
serve as his regent until he was old enough to   rule independently. A great deal of power could 
also be acquired by the families of consorts.   There was a hierarchy of these women, the most 
important of whom were queens or empresses;   and the rank of a consort determined her son’s 
place in the succession to the throne. Eunuchs,   on the other hand, had originally been castrated 
as a punishment for various crimes, but some of   them became important officials of the court, 
possibly because their infertility meant they   could not found their own dynasties; and ambitious 
men began to undergo this procedure voluntarily.   During the Han period, some of these court 
eunuchs used their influence for corrupt purposes,   which put them at odds with government officials 
who were adherents of Confucianism and believed   in rational and fair government. During the 160s 
CE, a conflict broke out between the two groups in   which the eunuchs were able to have the officials 
and their student supporters at the Imperial   University detained, and in some cases executed 
in what were called the “Partisan Prohibitions”.  The restrictions placed upon these Confucian 
officials lasted until the reign of Emperor Ling,   when the court decided to forgive them out of 
concern that they would join an uprising of   peasants that broke out in 184 CE. This uprising, 
called the “Yellow Turban Rebellion” after the   headgear worn by the rebels, happened because 
many peasants had lost their land due to famine   in the north. At the same time, they along 
with army veterans who could not find jobs   were being heavily taxed to pay for government 
building projects, while the eunuchs of the court   were being accused of widespread corruption. The 
rebellion, which took decades to suppress, was led   not by peasants but by three brothers who were the 
leaders of a Taoist sect that ministered to the   peasants and saw firsthand how the government was 
mistreating them. In the same year, a Taoist state   that had been founded to the north of the Sichuan 
province also rebelled against the Han, and for   several decades it was politically independent.
Beginning in 189 CE, a series of battles were   fought between the generals who were opposed 
to the power a group of eunuchs was wielding   over the imperial court, and the generals who 
supported them. This was followed in 200 by a   struggle between the general Yuan Shao and the 
minister Cao Cao over control of the Han emperor   Xian. Though Cao was defeated in 208, his son Cao 
Pi was able to force Xian to give up the throne to   him in the year 220; but rather than a unified 
government, the state he established became   one of three kingdoms into which the former 
Han empire was split for the next 60 years.  Han society was divided into 20 classes that 
included everyone between the imperial family   and the slaves. Each of these classes had its 
own privileges, and the highest were given both   a government pension and their own lands. Below 
government officials and scholars were landowners,   doctors, craftsmen, and merchants. There were 
also poor farmers who worked other people’s land.  The Han government was also a hierarchy made up 
of several layers. At the top was the emperor   himself, who was not limited by law but had 
a council of advisers whose decisions he was   expected to take seriously. He also had three 
councilors, and below them nine ministers. The   councilors, whose duties changed over time, 
were in charge of managing the state budget,   appointing high officials, reviewing reports 
from the provinces, and supervising public   works and military matters. The responsibilities 
of the ministers were more clearly delineated.   They included religious ceremonies, the 
emperor’s security, the imperial guards,   maintenance of horses and carriages, 
the administration of justice, receiving   foreign dignitaries, relations with the imperial 
family, finance, and the emperor’s personal needs.  The empire itself was divided up into 
administrative units from large provinces   to hamlets of 100 families. The provincial 
governors issued reports about the officials in   the regions under their control; while more local 
officials were in charge of finding people fit for   government service, raising troops when necessary, 
maintaining law and order, keeping tax records,   and organizing the labor required of each 
subject, which amounted to one month out   of the year. There was also a parallel system of 
administration for the “kingdoms” ruled over by   members of the royal family. These initially had 
a great deal of independence from the capital;   but in the mid-2nd century BCE, after a number 
of kings had rebelled and allied themselves with   the tribes of the Xiongnu, the emperor Jing 
took away their councilors and ministers,   and appointed their high officials himself.
The Han dynasty had an elaborate system of   taxation which funded its building, irrigation, 
and defensive projects. Taxes on land were   collected as a percentage of crops, while 
individuals also had to pay a personal tax which   was higher for adults than it was for children. 
Merchants, who were looked at with distaste by   the higher orders, were taxed more than others 
because the government wanted to keep them from   becoming too wealthy and powerful; and though they 
were expected to deal only in money, and at one   point were barred by law from buying land, some 
of them were able to become rich property owners.  The period of the Three Kingdoms ended in 280 
CE, when members of the Sima clan seized power   over Cao Wei, the state founded by the Cao 
family. They then founded the Jin dynasty by   conquering the other two kingdoms; but after 
Wu, its first emperor, died in 290, fighting   broke out over his succession, and a group of 
nomadic tribes including the Xiongnu invaded.   This forced the dynasty to abandon northern 
China and resettle in the vicinity of Nanjing,   which became its new capital. For the next 100 
years, there was an uneasy relationship between   these rulers from the north and the aristocrats 
who came with them, and the southerners over whom   they had placed themselves; and there were 
frequent rebellions within the military and   elsewhere, while several emperors gained power by 
murdering their predecessors. At the same time,   northern China was broken up into a group of 
sixteen kingdoms ruled by the tribes that had   invaded it; and these continued to hold power 
until a unified northern kingdom was established   early in the 5th century CE. But mainland China 
as a whole did not become a unified empire again   until the Tang dynasty of the 7th century, 
which has since come to be considered a high   point of Chinese culture. We will return 
to discuss this era later in the series.

## 40. Hydroformylation of Alkenes
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 5K | **Date:** 2 months ago | **Duration:** 6:47 | **ID:** bdq2-fQhRV0

We learned about syngas in the previous tutorial 
on the Fischer-Tropsch process, developed by   German chemists, which involves the liquefaction 
of charcoal. Now let’s learn about another   application for syngas. Hydroformylation is the 
addition of syngas, which once again is hydrogen   gas and carbon monoxide, to an alkene, usually a 
terminal one. Interestingly, hydroformylation was   discovered by another German chemist, Otto Roelen, 
in 1938, while working at the company Ruhrchemie   on further development of the Fischer-Tropsch 
reaction. This reaction also forms small amounts   of olefins, or alkenes, and Roelen noticed that 
syngas was adding to these alkenes to yield   aldehydes. He used a cobalt catalyst initially.
As you can see, a hydrogen atom is added to   one of the two olefin carbons, and a formyl 
group to the other. Two isomers are possible,   the branched, labeled B, and the linear one, 
labeled L. With the initial Roelen catalyst,   selectivity in favor of the linear isomer was 
modest, around 4:1 at best. Modification of the   catalyst with phosphines as ligands improved 
the selectivity to around 7 or 8:1, but still   required complex fractionation of the product by 
distillation. The conditions used were vigorous,   up to 170oC and 300 atmospheres of pressure.
In the late sixties, better catalysts were   developed based on rhodium 1. Rhodium is a much 
more expensive metal, but its catalysts are much   more selective, with over 90% linear selectivity. 
They are more durable, with up to 1,000 times the   number of turnovers possible than with cobalt, 
and much faster, so the temperatures used can be   milder, under 120oC, and the pressures required 
are easier to achieve, around 15-25 atmospheres.  The mechanism has been studied in detail and is 
generally similar for both cobalt and rhodium   catalysts. The species 1 usually has to lose a 
ligand in order to enter the catalytic cycle in   the form of 2. From there, the olefin coordinates 
to the metal center to yield 3. Then it undergoes   a hydrometalation to yield 4. This will undergo 
CO coordination to yield 5. This is followed by   insertion of CO into the rhodium-carbon bond to 
give formation of acyl-rhodium complex 6. Then,   oxidative addition of hydrogen gas yields 7. 
Finally, this undergoes reductive elimination   to yield the product 8, and also regenerate 
catalyst 2, which enters a new cycle.  The ligand has undergone major evolution over the 
years. Initially triphenylphosphine ligands were   used, but it was soon discovered that bidentate 
ligands yield better linear/branched ratios. For   example, butanal can be obtained in greater 
than 98% regioselectivity using the bidentate   ligand shown here. To screen ligands, 
it is advantageous to start with a Rh(I)   species containing a simple group, usually 
acetoacetate, abbreviated as acac. This is   activated by hydrogen gas to release acetoacetic 
acid while forming, upon addition of a ligand,   the Rh-H species depicted as 2 in the scheme from 
before. These precatalysts make the screening   of complex ligands especially convenient.
This reaction is very important industrially, as   the linear aldehydes are often immediately reduced 
to the parent alcohols, which are used in the   manufacturing of detergents and other products. 
The output of aldehydes by hydroformylation   has reached 7 million tons per year. Some 
companies use the cheaper cobalt catalysts,   others have industrialized the more efficient and 
selective rhodium process. In the latter case,   recovery of the metal is an essential part 
of the task to keep costs low. Just to give   you an idea of the efficiency of this complex 
process, butanal is available on the ton scale   for prices around $1 per kilogram. Not bad for 
a process using sophisticated rhodium catalysts   and fancy ligands. Lately, phosphite ligands 
have yielded exceptional selectivities for   terminal olefins. Here is an example from 
the labs of Steve Buchwald at MIT, where   essentially complete selectivity was obtained.
A specialty area is the hydroformylation of   internal alkenes. If the alkene is asymmetrical, 
mixtures inevitably arise. In some cases,   at high enough temperature and under very low 
CO pressures, rhodium hydride addition and beta   elimination can lead to migration of the double 
bond faster than hydroformylation. Given that   terminal olefins are hydroformylated 
much more rapidly than internal ones,   linear products can sometimes be obtained, as 
in this example by Piet van Leeuwen, working   at the University of Amsterdam.
In addition to its importance in the   chemical industry, hydroformylation has attracted 
the attention of synthetic organic chemists, which   have adapted this reaction towards the synthesis 
of complex molecules. In addition, chemists have   been fascinated by the linear selectivity of 
the reaction and have wondered whether, under   suitable conditions, branched products can be made 
to predominate. The branched products are, in most   cases, chiral, and therefore the possibility 
of enantioselective synthesis arises. One such   example is from the labs of Professor Kyoko Nozaki 
from the University of Tokyo. She has shown that   olefins substituted with polar substituents tend 
to give some branched selectivity, and she has   been able to optimize the ligands to achieve 
complete regioselectivity, and in some cases,   excellent enantioselectivity using this ligand.
In summary, hydroformylation is one of the most   important processes in the chemical industry, 
and it is also attracting the attention of   synthetic chemists, in particular those who are 
keen to apply enantioselective methodology to   the synthesis of valuable chiral intermediates. 
This is still an area of current research and new   results are reported with remarkable frequency. 
New metals are being applied to the reaction,   as well as new ligands. The number of publications 
in this area has reached around 300 per year,   and there are multivolume books 
dedicated to this topic. Thus,   hydroformylation, especially due to its industrial 
applications, is still a huge research field.

## 43. Diversity of the Ray-Finned Fishes Part 2: Teleosts (Modern Fish)
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 5K | **Date:** 2 months ago | **Duration:** 14:43 | **ID:** RoPuPkjTAGw
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=RoPuPkjTAGw

### Transcript:
In the previous tutorial we discussed 
the diversity of the ray-finned fishes,   and covered all species outside of the teleosts, 
or modern fish. Now let’s dive into the diversity   of the teleosts. The teleosts are first split 
into the clades Elopomorpha, Osteoglossomorpha,   and Clupeocephala. All members of Elopomorpha are 
unique in that they produce Leptocephalus larvae,   which are flat and transparent and contain a 
jelly-like substance on the inside of the body,   as well as a thin layer of muscle with visible 
myomeres on the outside. As juveniles, their body   organs are small and they have only a simple tube 
for a gut. In addition to a great deal of extinct   species, the extant elopomorphs include the 
tarpons, tenpounders, and ladyfish of Elopiformes,   which have slender, streamlined bodies that allow 
them to move efficiently through the water and   capture their prey. There are also the bonefishes 
of order Albuliformes, often noted for their   silver-colored bodies and deeply forked tails, 
the deep-sea spiny eels of Notacanthiformes,   and the true eels of Anguilliformes. The true 
eels are the most diverse clade of the superorder   elopomorpha. Note that this order includes the 
true eels only, such as the slender giant moray,   European conger, garden eels, pelican eels, 
gulpers, American eels, Japanese eels,   and snake eels. They swim by generating waves 
that travel the length of their bodies and can   swim backwards by reversing the direction of the 
wave. As adults, they possess no pelvic fins,   they have a dorsal fin and anal fin that are fused 
with the caudal fin, and many species also lack   pectoral fins. Most true eels are nocturnal and 
live as adults in the shallow waters of the ocean.  Next-up, Osteoglossomorpha, sometimes listed 
synonymously with the order Osteoglossiformes,   includes the mooneyes, often placed in their own 
order of Hiodontiformes, as well as the arapaima,   arowana, aba, and elephantfishes of order 
Osteoglossiformes. They are characterized by   their unique bony tongues, which have tooth-like 
structures and are used for capturing prey. Many,   like the arowana, are specially adapted to surface 
feeding and can leap up to six feet out of the   water after their food. Others, like the arapaima, 
are among the largest freshwater fish in the world   and can reach lengths of over 3 meters, or 
9.8 feet, and have a hard mineralized outer   surface. Still others, like the elephant fishes 
and aba can sense and produce electric charges   to aid in feeding and deter potential predators.
Clupeocephala, meanwhile, is further divided into   the clades Otocephala and Euteleostei. Members of 
Otocephala share a common characteristic called   the otolith, a small bone in the inner ear that 
aids in hearing and balance, fused to the second   vertebra of the backbone, meaning that the vast 
majority of these species are capable of hearing,   and many like the catfish communicate by sound. 
Otocephala species are found in both freshwater   and marine environments, and they exhibit a 
wide range of ecological roles and feeding   strategies. They include the herrings, sardines, 
and anchovies of order Clupeiformes, which are   highly abundant and widely distributed in both 
marine and freshwater environments, as well as   several smaller orders such as the slickheads of 
order Alepocephaliformes, characterized by their   elongated bodies, large mouths, and well-developed 
sensory organs. These inhabit the deep ocean,   and some, especially those of the genus 
Alepocephalus, have light-producing organs.  This clade also includes more diverse orders 
like the catfish of order Siluriformes,   named as such because of their prominent barbels, 
which resemble a cat's whiskers. However, not all   members of this order actually have “whiskers,” 
and they are instead defined by their heavy,   bony head, greatly reduced swim bladder, and 
their lack of scales. Even armored species,   with external bone plates, lack true scales. 
Catfish range in size from small species like   the glass catfish, all the way up to the massive 
piraíba, wels catfish, and Mekong giant catfish,   among others. Some, like the electric catfish can 
produce an electric charge. Contrary to popular   belief, the sensory barbels are harmless and 
cannot “sting,” but a number of catfish species   do have spine-like rays on their dorsal and 
pectoral fins that can deliver a stinging   venom if irritated. Some members, like those 
of the genus Heteropneustes can produce a venom   strong enough to cause hospitalization, and 
in rare cases, even lead to death. However,   the vast majority of all catfish 
species are harmless to humans.  In contrast, there are only a few extant 
species of order Gonorynchiformes,   which includes the milkfish, beaked salmon, 
shellears, and hingemouths. These are primarily   freshwater or brackish water species found 
in tropical and subtropical regions. They   are characterized by their elongated 
bodies and distinct beak-like snouts.  Order Cypriniformes includes a wide range of 
diverse and familiar species, such as the carps,   minnows, and loaches. They are essentially 
all “carp-like” fish and new species are   described on a nearly bi-monthly basis. A 
few common species include the common carp,   goldfish, zebrafish, including the first 
genetically modified GloFish, rosy barb,   common loach, fathead minnow, and Koi, which 
are actually colored varieties of the Amur carp.  Next, order Characiformes is an order of 
ray-finned fish that includes a diverse group of   species known for their vibrant colors and active 
behavior. These fish are predominantly found in   freshwater habitats of South America and Africa. 
Characiformes encompass popular aquarium species   like tetras, piranhas, and hatchetfish, known for 
their stunning appearance and schooling behavior.  And finally, members of order Gymnotiformes are 
commonly known as neotropical knifefish or South   American knifefish. They are easily recognized 
by their elongated bodies and anal fin and are   known for their unique ability to generate weak 
electric fields for communication, navigation,   and hunting. They include the electric eels, 
which can produce high and low voltage using   their three different electric organs, which 
are capable of concentrating their discharge,   thus producing a shock painful enough 
to stun or deter virtually any predator.  Backing up a bit, Euteleostei includes several 
orders that are often regarded as sister taxa   to the large and diverse clade Neoteleostei. The 
order Lepidogalaxiiformes includes a single extant   species of endangered small fish native to Western 
Australia commonly known as the salamanderfish.  Esociformes get their name from pikes of the 
genus Esox. They also include the mudminnows   and various extinct species. Many members of this 
clade, and the pikes in particular, have sharp,   pointed heads and pointed teeth, and are 
often apex predators in their ecosystems,   feeding on smaller fish and other 
aquatic prey. The northern pike   and muskellunge are well-known members 
of this order, and are highly prized by   anglers for their size and fighting ability.
Order Salmoniformes includes salmon, trout,   and char. These fish are primarily found in cold 
and temperate waters of the Northern Hemisphere,   both in freshwater and marine environments. They 
are known for their migratory behavior, with many   species undertaking long-distance migrations for 
spawning. Salmoniformes have streamlined bodies,   powerful tails, and are well adapted for swimming 
against strong currents. They are carnivorous   predators of the middle food chain, feeding on 
small crustaceans, aquatic insects, tadpoles,   and smaller fish, and in turn are preyed upon by 
larger predators. Many species are thus considered   keystone species important for both 
freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems due   to the biomass transfer provided by their mass 
migration from oceanic to inland waterbodies.  Order Argentiniformes has only recently been 
recognized as a separate order and includes   the marine smelts and the deep sea barreleyes.
Order Galaxiiformes includes a single family of   mainly small freshwater fish that are widely 
distributed in the Southern hemisphere,   most of which live in Southern Australia and 
New Zealand. They include the common galaxias,   which is one of the most widely distributed 
fish species in the Southern hemisphere.  Members of order Stomiiformes are commonly 
referred to as dragonfish and allies,   and they include many deep-sea fishes of extremely 
diverse morphology, from the lightfishes to the   loosejaws, marine hatchetfishes, and viper 
fish. Nearly all members of this order are   capable of biolumination through photophores, 
and many migrate daily in the water column.  Finally, order Osmeriformes includes the true 
smelts, known for their slender bodies and   streamlined shapes, and ability to form 
large schools and feed on small prey,   such as plankton and small fish. Some species 
of Osmeriformes, like the European smelt   (Osmerus eperlanus), are commercially 
important and support local fisheries.  Moving forward, there are just three orders that 
are part of Neoteleostei, but not Acanthomorpha.   They are Ateleopodiformes, Aulopiformes, and 
Myctophiformes. Members of order Ateleopodiformes   includes about a dozen species known as jellynose 
fishes or tadpole fishes, which are deep-water,   bottom-dwelling, marine fishes, extant species 
of which all have skeletons made of cartilage,   and large bulbous heads. Order Aulopiformes 
includes mainly deep-sea species, members   of which are commonly referred to as ginners 
or lizardfishes. Many of these have either a   vestigial swim bladder or lack one entirely. 
Many species have a distinct appearance with   long jaws and sharp teeth, which they use to 
capture small fish and invertebrates. They   vary from relatively small species to the rather 
large, fast moving, predatory lancetfish. Finally,   Myctophiformes also includes deep-sea species such 
as the often highly abundant lanternfish and the   blackchins. Overall, they are small fishes 
that are laterally compressed and often have   large eyes, photophores, and large mouths.
Moving forward, Acanthomorpha, which means   “thorn-shaped”, includes nearly 15,000 species 
of ray-finned fish split into 9 smaller orders,   and the extremely large and diverse clade 
Percomorpha. Polymixiiformes includes a   single extant genus of beardfishes, named 
for their pair of long hyoid barbels.   Order Percopsiformes includes the trout-perches, 
which are small, freshwater fish primarily found   in North America, with elongated bodies, large 
eyes, and are often mistaken for other species.   Members of order Zeiformes are often commonly 
referred to as dories, and have distinctive   disc-shaped bodies along with a single dorsal fin 
that extends along most of their back that contain   a series of sharp spines. Order Stylephoriformes 
contains only a single species found in deep   tropical waters around the world, known as 
the tube-eye or thread-tail. Though it may   look threatening, it is actually a filter feeder 
that sucks seawater by enlarging its oral cavity   to about 40 times its original size, and then 
expels the water through the gills, leaving behind   the copepods on which it feeds. Order Gadiformes 
includes several species of economically important   fish collectively known as cod. They are found 
in both saltwater and freshwater environments,   with many species inhabiting cold or deep-sea 
regions. They have spineless fins and range   in size from the miniscule codlets up to the 
Atlantic Cod. Order Lampriformes includes the   ribbonfish, opahs, oarfish, and crestfishes, many 
of which are characterized by their ribbon-like   appearance with elongated bodies that are 
typically brightly-colored and contain between 84   and 96 vertebrae, as well as long characteristic 
dorsal fins that extend most of the length of   the body. Order Trachichthyiformes includes 
the fangtooth, spinyfin, lanterneye fishes,   pinecone fishes, and slime heads. As a group, they 
are characterized by their unique body shapes,   often with elongated and compressed 
bodies. Many, especially the slimeheads,   are deep-sea dwellers with long lifespans. Order 
Beryciformes includes the whalefishes, ridgeheads,   and alfonsinos. They are primarily nocturnal, and 
the whalefish in particular are noted for their   large mouths, and small pectoral and pelvic fins. 
Order Holocentriformes includes the soldierfish   and squirrelfish. Like the Beryciformes, many 
species are either entirely or partly nocturnal.   They are noted for their relatively large eyes, 
as well as red, orange, and silver coloration.  And finally, Percomorpha, or Percomorphaceae, 
sometimes simply listed as Perciformes,   is a large clade of ray-finned fish 
that contains more species than the   entire class of mammals. However, not only is 
this clade incredibly diverse, it’s also very   complicated and still undergoing revision. So 
let’s move forward and check out this clade next.

Over several tutorials, we have discussed 
different fingerprint patterns and their   individual characteristics. Now let’s find out 
how fingerprints are deposited on a surface. To   avoid confusion between actual fingerprints on 
your hand and the ones deposited on a surface,   we shall use the term fingermarks for the 
latter. Fingermarks are formed as a result   of the interaction between the surface and 
the fingerprint. Broadly, we can classify   the fingermarks into three types. One: plastic 
prints. These are three-dimensional fingermarks   formed when a finger is pressed against a soft 
surface, such as clay, wax, wet paint, wet soap,   et cetera. Two: patent prints. These are 
two-dimensional fingermarks that form when   fingers that are carrying a particular material 
such as wet paint, blood, or ink, are pressed   against a surface. Such fingermarks are readily 
visible on many surfaces. Three: latent prints.   These are also two-dimensional fingermarks, but 
they are not easily visible to the naked eye. Just   turn off your smartphone screen for a while. 
At first glance, you might not be able to see   anything. However, you will be able to visualize 
the fingermarks on your screen when you tilt it   at some angle. How are these fingermarks formed? 
Can you recall which principle of forensic science   is at play here? It is Locard’s law of exchange, 
which says that “every contact leaves a trace”.   According to this law, these fingermarks are 
a result of the mutual exchange of material   between your fingerprints and the screen. A 
detailed study of all these interactions is   important to determine the probability of finding 
fingermarks at the crime scene. Latent fingermarks   are not readily visible. However, they can be 
successfully recovered from almost any surface   only if the right technique is applied. The 
nature of different surfaces will influence the   techniques used to locate fingermarks. The surface 
of a doorknob is one of the most plausible places   to find a fingermark at the CS. But fingermarks 
on it might not be visible to the naked eye.   So, should the surface just be ignored during 
evidence collection? If this is done, valuable   evidence present at the CS will be contaminated. 
The presence of fingermarks can almost certainly   establish the presence of a party at the CS. 
If the investigators fail in locating them,   it can heavily influence the case at trial. This 
is why the knowledge of these interactions is of   utmost importance. Let us discuss them in detail.
The process of deposition of any fingermark   generally involves three stages. One: 
application of the finger on a surface. Here,   positive pressure is applied by the finger to the 
surface due to which both of them get deformed   to some extent. Two: transfer of material. 
In this stage, the finger and the surface   are in contact with each other. Material gets 
exchanged between the finger and the surface.   The extent of transfer will depend on different 
factors such as the nature of the surface,   the constituents present on the surface and the 
applied finger, duration of time for which the   finger was applied, and so forth. Three: removal 
of the finger from the surface. With this stage,   the process of transfer gets completed. Both 
the finger and the surface get relaxed to their   original state. The result of this process is 
not only the formation of fingermarks on the   surface but also constituents from the surface 
getting picked up by the fingers. Based on   these interactions, fingermarks can be classified 
into positive and negative impressions. Positive   impressions are formed when the residue carried 
by the ridges of the finger gets deposited on a   surface. Therefore, the lines of the resultant 
fingermark correspond to the actual ridges of   the fingerprint, and the empty spaces between the 
lines resemble the furrows of the fingerprint.   The visibility of positive fingermarks will 
depend on the nature of fingerprint residue,   the color and reflexivity of the surface, lighting 
conditions, and more. If the fingermark is easily   visible, it is a patent print. If the fingermark 
is not visible without additional treatments,   it is classified as a latent print. A patent 
print like a bloodstained fingermark can be easily   recognized and recovered during the investigation. 
Nonetheless, it is not always the case that an   investigator will find abundant patent prints on 
a crime scene. On the other hand, latent prints   can be collected from any type of surface if the 
correct technique is adopted. Just because they   are invisible does not mean they are not present.
Going back to the fingermarks on your smartphone   screen, now that we have established that they are 
latent marks, do you wonder what residue might be   present in them? Let’s discuss what the friction 
ridge residue is made of. A major proportion of   fingermarks consist of sweat. The sweat glands 
present on our palms, the eccrine glands,   secrete sweat which is made up of different 
constituents such as urea, creatinine, amino   acids, different proteins, and so forth. Another 
type of sweat gland is the apocrine gland situated   in our armpits and genital areas. Sometimes our 
fingerprints seem oily or greasy. This is due   to the presence of sebum in the residue, which 
are fatty acids secreted by the sebaceous glands   located in our face and hair follicles. We tend 
to touch different body parts arbitrarily. We   scratch our heads and touch our faces very often, 
which deposits oil and sweat on the fingerprints.   Therefore, though apocrine sweat and sebum are 
not directly secreted by the palmar region,   they are largely present in our fingerprints as a 
result of this constant transfer. Similarly, other   external contaminants become a part of fingerprint 
residue resulting from our interactions with our   environment. Sometimes contaminants present in 
the fingermark such as residue from nicotine,   cosmetics, dust, grease, and foodstuffs, can also 
point towards the lifestyle of the person. So,   now when you look at your fingerprint 
impressions on the smartphone screen,   think of all these residues that make them. An 
awareness regarding the constituents present   in the fingerprints will help us determine 
their affinity towards a particular surface.   This relative affinity will decide the 
further protocol of recovery. For example,   fingerprints having greater moisture content would 
be easily recovered from a non-porous surface such   as a surface made of plastic or rubber. But 
the same approach wouldn't be applicable for   a porous surface such as paper. In the upcoming 
tutorials, we’ll be studying different methods of   fingerprint detection and enhancement according 
to the nature of the residue present in it.  With positive fingermarks covered, let’s not 
forget about negative marks. Negative marks   are formed when the ridges carry residue from 
the surface as opposed to the positive marks in   which ridges deposit residue. Go to any place 
in your room that has gathered dust over time,   like a bookshelf. Touch the dusty area and observe 
the resultant pattern under oblique lighting.   Because the ridges have picked up the dust, 
the lines on the fingermark will correspond to   the furrows of the fingerprint, whereas the blank 
spaces between them will correspond to the ridges.   Negative impressions are not generally found on

of fingerprint impressions, plastic prints,   these are a result of fingers pressing into a 
soft surface and permanently deforming it. Being   a three-dimensional impression, the quality 
of this print is primarily dependent on the   texture of the surface, pressure applied by the 
finger, and the presence of other contaminants.   They are not frequently found on a crime scene 
when compared to latent and patent prints.  With that, we now understand the dynamics 
behind fingerprint deposition. With all the   fundamentals of fingerprint science covered, we

## 46. Ancient China Part 2: The Zhou Dynasty (1000 – 200 BCE)
**Channel:** Professor Dave Explains | **Views:** 10K | **Date:** 2 months ago | **Duration:** 11:03 | **ID:** el7LytzY3h4
**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=el7LytzY3h4

### Transcript:
The economic, technological, and cultural 
developments that took place in northern   China during the first millennium BCE may 
not specifically be assigned to either the   Shang dynasty, which we discussed in the 
previous tutorial, or the first part of   the Zhou dynasty that came after it, because the 
innovations of the Shang period continued and were   developed further in the Zhou kingdom of the 11th 
through the 8th centuries BCE. This era is known   as the “Western Zhou” to distinguish it from the 
“Eastern Zhou” of the 8th through 3rd centuries,   when many political, social and economic changes 
took place. During the Western Zhou, the outlying   parts of the empire were largely left to govern 
themselves in accordance with the principle of   fengjian or “grant and establishment”, which gave 
local aristocrats control of the lands to the   east of the kingdom’s heartland in exchange 
for a share of their agricultural produce,   and an oath of loyalty to the king which would 
be put into practice in times of war or invasion.   These nobles were given one of a number of titles 
that reflected their seniority, from duke, or   gong, down to baron, or nan; though as they grew 
more independent over the course of the dynasty,   their actual power had little to do with their 
assigned rank. Below the nobility were the local   aristocracy, the merchants, the workers, and 
finally the peasants, to whom the king gave a   share in the available farmland for them to work 
themselves; while other shares were given to the   nobles who hired others to work it for them. 
Professions were hereditary in the sense that   the eldest son would take up his father’s work. 
The fengjian states had their own systems of   justice and taxation, and even their own forms of 
money; and because this form of government came to   be associated with the philosophy of Confucius, 
it was seen by later eras of Chinese history as   an ideal of political organization. But alongside 
this decentralization, the concept of the Mandate   of Heaven solidified the place of the king, while 
leaving open the possibility that a king who was   seen as a failure might be overthrown on the 
grounds that he had lost his divine support.  There were further developments in technology, 
economy, and infrastructure during the Zhou   period. Irrigation works were expanded, and trade 
increased as new roads and canals were built.   These projects were made possible by the 
development of more centralized and professional   bureaucracies within the vassal states, which 
made good use of the wealth they acquired from   agriculture and taxation. The technique of forging 
iron, which would become an essential resource for   producing weapons, appeared by the 6th century; 
and the writing system also developed further from   the form that was used on the Shang oracle bones.
The Zhou period is also famous for the works   of literature it produced. The Zhou Yi, which 
acts as the core of the I Ching, a text used to   understand the will of Heaven, which also became 
a philosophical work, was composed at this time,   legendarily ascribed to the brother of Wu, 
the first Zhou king. The poems included in   the Classic of Poetry, one of the “Five Classics” 
later attributed to Confucius, were also composed   during the Western Zhou. Confucianism 
in general, in the sense of a philosophy   that promotes social order and self-improvement, 
became a dominant belief, though it was suppressed   during the Qin dynasty that followed the Zhou.
Over the course of the Western Zhou period, the   fengjian system gradually broke down as the local 
nobles, who had originally been close relatives   of the king but were now much more distantly 
connected to him, became entirely independent   of the royal court. It came to an end along with 
the Western Zhou in the 8th century BCE, when one   of these nobles, the Marquis of Shen, went to 
war with King You, who had married the Marquis’   daughter to cement their alliance, but threw her 
aside in favor of another woman. After defeating   You with the help of a nomadic tribe, the Marquis 
installed his own grandson as the new king,   and the capital was moved eastward to Wangcheng.
The Eastern Zhou is traditionally divided into   two periods. The first, which lasted until the 
early 5th century BCE, is named the “Spring   and Autumn” after a work by that name which 
chronicles one of the Zhou states during this   era, and is another of the Five Classics 
associated with Confucius. During this period,   conflict with the Zhou kings developed into open 
war. At the end of the 8th century, the state   of Zheng attacked the army of King Huan during 
a dispute over territory, injuring the king,   and his successor was nearly assassinated by the 
members of his own court. The dukes who ruled the   vassal states fought both foreign enemies, like 
the barbarian Rong people, and each other; though   a group of twelve dukes decided to form a council 
in order to coordinate their joint foreign policy.   This council was led by the state with the most 
powerful army, which was appointed over the others   by the king. During the 7th century, a series 
of different dukes were given this appointment.  At first, the lack of central authority allowed 
the fengjian to splinter into around 150 states,   which were often no larger than a single 
city; but over time, the smaller states were   absorbed by the larger ones until only four 
of them were left. These were Chu, Qin, Jin,   and Qi. Early in the 6th century they attempted 
to cease fighting by stabilizing their borders,   but they were not successful. There were also 
conflicts between elite families of the individual   states. In the 5th century, the powerful state 
of Jin was divided up between the Han, Zhao,   and Wei clans, which then became separate powers.
It was during the late 6th century that the figure   Sun Tzu, who may have been a later invention, was 
said to have developed the strategic ideas that   would eventually be compiled in the Art of War, 
in the hopes that good military tactics would   allow some of the vassal states to defeat the 
others, and bring an end to constant warfare.  But even though the Spring and Autumn and Warring 
States periods are often associated with conflict   and chaos, they are also considered the most 
fruitful age of Chinese philosophy, which is   called the “Hundred Schools of Thought” because 
it gave birth to several different philosophies.   Confucius, who became so influential that all 
of the anonymous literary and philosophical   works of the time were later attributed to him, 
lived in the second half of the 6th century;   while Lao Tzu, who is traditionally considered 
the author of the Taoist work Tao Te Ching,   was believed to be his contemporary, though 
he may actually have lived during the Warring   States period. Taoism offered an alternative to 
Confucianism by promoting a way of life that was   spontaneous and in accordance with nature, rather 
than one grounded in social order and ritual.  In addition to Confucianism and Taoism, the most 
influential schools of the time were Legalism and   Mohism. Legalism saw human beings as inherently 
uncooperative and disrespectful of authority,   so rather than encouraging the sort of 
individual responsibility and decency that   Confucius advocated, it promoted the use of law 
to force people into treating each other properly,   and privileged the desires of the state over 
those of the people. On the other hand, Mohism   emphasized the importance of universal respect, a 
modest way of life, pacifism in relations between   states, as well as the obedience of subjects to 
their rulers, and rulers to the will of Heaven.  The second half of the Eastern Zhou, 
which is called the “Warring States”,   was a time of constant conflict between the 
vassal states of the Zhou empire, which were   by then functionally independent. At the same 
time, these states continued to recognize the   Zhou monarch as their figurehead, although he no 
longer controlled even his own original territory;   this meant that the court could not draft its 
own armies, and had to rely on its vassal states   for its defense. During this period, between 
the 5th and 3rd centuries, conflict escalated   into outright war as seven states absorbed the 
others and then fought one another for control.   Three of these had been part of the state of 
Jin, until its leading families divided it up   into separate kingdoms. The rulers of these 
states increasingly rejected the traditional   belief in the Zhou mandate of Heaven, to the 
point that during the mid and late 5th century,   five of them: the rulers of Qi, Wei, Qin, Han, 
and Yan, declared themselves kings. They also made   changes to their armies, making more use of iron 
weapons, replacing composite bows with crossbows,   and adopting the cavalry tactics they learned 
from northern nomadic groups like the Xiongnu.  As these large states became more powerful 
militarily, they also became more centralized and   bureaucratic. Adopting the principles of Legalism, 
they reduced the power of local aristocrats and   replaced them with officials chosen from the 
lower classes for their skills and training.   In the middle of the 4th century, the state of Qin 
changed many of its economic, social, and military   policies. Its chief minister, Shang Yang, decreed 
that farmers whose crop yields exceeded the quotas   imposed on them would be rewarded with slaves 
taken from farmers who failed to meet them. He   also encouraged farmers from other states to move 
to Qin, and drafted peasants into its army. Young   people were forced to marry and given financial 
incentives to have more children; and families   were taxed if their sons lived together in the 
same household rather than starting their own.   The increased population and agricultural 
production that resulted from these policies led   the Zhao king to appoint the duke of Qin over his 
other vassals; and it soon defeated Wei in battle   and annexed a great deal of its territory.
In the first half of the 3rd century,   Qin went on to defeat the states of Chu, 
Han, and then Zhao, which was the only   other major power at that point. Finally, in 
251 BCE, Zhuangxiang, the king of Qin, invaded   what remained of Zhou territory and received the 
mandate of Heaven. Between the years 230 and 221,   his son Zheng conquered the states of Han, Wei, 
Chu, Zhao, Yan, and Qi, and with these victories   a single dynastic state was formed, making Qin 
the first Chinese dynasty. Though it would turn   out to be very short-lived, it served as a model 
of political and social organization for the more   successful Han dynasty that followed it, and for 
the rest of Chinese history until the modern era.

One of the more interesting industrial processes 
ever invented, the synthesis of petroleum from   coal, was developed, like most other chemical 
processes of the early 20th century, by German   chemists. Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch, working 
at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Coal Research   in Mülheim an der Ruhr, were tasked with 
converting charcoal, which was abundant   in Germany, into petroleum, the critical fuel for 
transportation at the time, something Germany did   not produce in sufficient amounts to sustain their 
needs. Their breakthrough was announced in 1926,   and was rapidly applied all over the world on an 
industrial scale. It became especially important   to the Nazi regime, which needed large amounts 
of fuel in order to sustain war preparations.  The process consists of the catalytic conversion 
of syngas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and   hydrogen, into hydrocarbons, which act as fuel 
for modern gasoline engines. Syngas was obtained,   at that time, primarily through the gasification 
of charcoal using steam at high temperature.   That is shown here, where coal, which 
is elemental carbon, reacts with water,   to produce carbon monoxide and hydrogen 
gas, or syngas. Then in a second reaction,   carbon monoxide reacts with hydrogen gas in the 
presence of a catalyst at high temperature and   pressure to produce hydrocarbons of varying length 
and water. This is the Fischer-Tropsch process.  The catalysts consist of fine metal particles 
immobilized on an inert matrix, usually silica   or alumina. The metal itself is usually iron 
or cobalt. Ruthenium also works, but it is   more expensive, whereas nickel has much lower 
chain growth reactivity. Each metal has its own   advantages and drawbacks, with formation of many 
possible unwanted products such as methane, which   offers no chain growth, olefins, alcohols and 
ketones, which are less energetic, and aromatics.   Catalyst optimization is still an active area 
of research. The temperatures can reach 350oC   and the pressure can be up to several bars.
The hydrogen to carbon monoxide ratio is very   important for an optimum yield of hydrocarbon. 
It is usually adjusted to the desired level,   around 2:1, by increasing the temperature 
until the water-gas shift reaction becomes   significant. This reduces the level of CO 
and increases the level of H2. Unfortunately,   carbon dioxide is also produced in the reaction.
Now let’s discuss the mechanism. It is fairly   well understood how hydrogen is activated by 
metals, and we have already covered this in an   earlier hydrogenation tutorial. Essentially, 
the H-H bond is broken at the metal surface,   and metal-hydride moieties are created, 
with the hydride being able to diffuse   quickly across the surface. Carbon monoxide 
is activated to generate oxocarbide complexes,   which are in equilibrium with a bridge-mode 
bound CO molecule. Both species may contribute   to catalysis. From these oxocarbide complexes, two 
hydrides could add to form a hydroxyalkyl complex,   which is further reduced to a methylene group 
by two further hydrides, releasing water. Next,   several vicinal methylene groups are joined 
to form C-C bonds, followed by reduction and   release of the hydrocarbon, in this case butane. 
In the case of the bridged CO, the initial species   is split, resulting in M carbide complexes and 
metal-oxo complexes. These are both hydrogenated   by bound hydrides, the oxo-complex to water, 
which is desorbed, and the carbide to methylene,   which can polymerize as in the previous example.
The product distribution in the Fischer-Tropsch   process is complex, since many different 
hydrocarbons can be produced. As we mentioned,   an undesired product is methane, by double 
hydride addition to an M-methylene residue,   because it is not liquid. Efforts to avoid this 
have produced long-chain paraffins, which are   waxy solids and are therefore also undesirable in 
liquid fuels. Usually parameters are adjusted so   as to avoid waxes, targeting hydrocarbons of ten 
carbons or less, meaning that n-decane is usually   the longest linear alkane that is acceptable.
An interesting approach to syngas is the thermal   gasification of biomass. Under appropriate 
conditions, biomass, primarily a mixture   of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, 
can be transformed into syngas, and this   can be fed into a suitable Fischer-Tropsch 
reactor, producing bio-renewable gasoline.   Given that petroleum will account for over 80% of 
our energy needs until 2040, the Fischer-Tropsch   process may help us significantly to 
navigate the next few decades before   our energy sources switch to carbon-neutral.
There are already many production plants in   the world using the chemistry we just described. 
The largest is in South Africa, managed by the   company Sasol, which produces 165,000 barrels 
of gasoline per day using the Fischer-Tropsch   process. This is, of course, not particularly 
significant in terms of global oil consumption,   as it represents only 0.17% of the daily world 
supply. Nevertheless, the technology has proven   itself highly cost-effective and practical. This 
chemistry is still the subject of optimization   research, as new production plants are brought 
online constantly throughout the world.  Finally, it is widely believed that this process 
is relevant to the origin of life. It has been   suggested that long chain aliphatic molecules, 
like for example fatty acids, may have originated   by naturally occurring hot metal surfaces 
acting as natural sources of syngas followed   by some oxidative process. Thus, nature may have 
devised this chemistry long before Fischer and   Tropsch thought of the idea, and may have used 
it to enable the appearance of life on earth.
